title: Consider memory system with 32-bit address. Cache size is 512KB
subject: COA
text: Consider a memory system with 32-bit address. Cache size is 512KB and cache uses line size of 64 Bytes. Cache is 4-way set associative. Determine the number of TAG bits in the main memory address bits.
solution:
Given the parameters of the memory system:

Address bits: 32 bits

Cache size: 512 KB

Line size: 64 Bytes

4-way set associative cache

To determine the number of TAG bits:

Cache size = 512 KB = 512 * 1024 Bytes = 524288 Bytes.
Number of cache lines = Cache size / Line size = 524288 / 64 = 8192 lines.
Number of sets in the cache = 8192 / 4 (since 4-way associative) = 2048 sets.
Index bits = log₂(Number of sets) = log₂(2048) = 11 bits.
Block offset bits = log₂(Line size) = log₂(64) = 6 bits.
Total address bits = 32 bits.
TAG bits = Total address bits - (Index bits + Block offset bits) = 32 - (11 + 6) = 15 bits.

title: The main memory of computer has blocks while the cache
subject: COA
text: The main memory of a computer has 2cm blocks while the cache has 2c blocks. If the cache uses the set-associative mapping scheme with two blocks per set, then block k of the main memory maps to the set:
solution:
In set-associative mapping, a cache is partitioned into equal-size sets and each main-memory block is assigned to exactly one set. The governing rule is: set index = (block number) mod (number of cache sets). The modulus is the number of sets, not the number of cache blocks.

Applying the rule to this item:

  1. Notation check: 2c and 2cm in the source are ordinary products, 2 × c and 2 × c × m; they are not powers of 2.

  2. Cache size: the cache contains 2c blocks.

  3. Associativity: two blocks are stored in each set.

  4. Number of sets: S = (2c cache blocks) / (2 blocks per set) = c.

  5. Mapping: block k is assigned to set k mod c.

Therefore, block k of main memory maps to set (k mod c) of the cache.

Contrast with the other values:

  • (k mod m) uses the main-memory multiplier m rather than the cache-set count.

  • (k mod 2c) uses the total number of cache blocks before grouping them two per set.

  • (k mod 2cm) uses the total number of main-memory blocks rather than the cache-set count.

Cross-check: 2cm main-memory blocks distributed across c sets give 2cm / c = 2m candidate blocks per set, which is consistent with c cache sets.

optionFeedback.html: Using m as the modulus partitions main-memory block numbers into m residue classes: k is assigned according to its remainder on division by m.
Using c as the modulus partitions main-memory block numbers into c residue classes: k is assigned according to its remainder on division by c.
Using 2c as the modulus partitions main-memory block numbers into 2c residue classes: k is assigned according to its remainder on division by 2c.
Using 2cm as the modulus partitions main-memory block numbers into 2cm residue classes: k is assigned according to its remainder on division by 2cm.

title: Consider cache memory organization with lines in which the cache
subject: COA
text: Consider a nontrivial cache memory organization with m > 1 lines in which the cache is divided into v sets, each of which consists of k lines. The set-associative mapping reduces to direct mapping when:
solution:
CONCEPT — A v-set, k-way set-associative cache contains m = v × k cache lines. Direct mapping is the one-way special case: every set contains exactly one candidate cache line, so k = 1.

APPLICATION — For the stated nontrivial cache, substituting k = 1 into m = v × k gives m = v × 1 = v. Therefore the matching pair is v = m and k = 1.

CONTRAST — The remaining pairs describe different organizations or capacities:

  • v = m and k = m gives v × k = m² lines, not the stated m lines when m > 1.

  • v = 1 and k = m gives one set holding all m lines, the fully associative case.

  • v = 1 and k = 1 gives a one-line cache, which conflicts with the stated m > 1 capacity.

CROSS-CHECK — With v = m and k = 1, each block index selects exactly one of m sets, and that set contains exactly one line. This reproduces the defining placement rule of a direct-mapped cache.

optionFeedback.html: For v = m and k = m, the cache has m sets, m lines per set, and a total capacity of m² lines.
For v = 1 and k = m, the cache has one set, m lines per set, and a total capacity of m lines; all lines belong to the same set.
For v = m and k = 1, the cache has m sets, one line per set, and a total capacity of m lines; each set contains one candidate line.
For v = 1 and k = 1, the cache has one set, one line per set, and a total capacity of one line.

title: 4-way set-associative cache has blocks and block size of bytes.
subject: COA
text: A 4-way set-associative cache has 256 blocks and a block size of 16 bytes. How many sets are present in the cache?

optionFeedback.html: Correct. Applying the structural formula 256 blocks / 4{blocks/set} yields exactly 64 separate sets contained inside the cache storage.
Incorrect. This value represents the block size in bytes (16 bytes), which relates to line offset calculations rather than the spatial division of blocks into sets.
Incorrect. This value would be the result if the cache were 2-way set-associative (256 / 2), but the question explicitly specifies a 4-way set-associative design.
Incorrect. This value does not match any valid structural division parameter of the blocks under a 4-way set-associative mapping scheme.

title: In k-way set associative cache the cache is divided into
subject: COA
text: In a k-way set associative cache, the cache is divided into v sets, each of which consists of k lines. The lines of a set are placed in sequence one after another. The lines in set s are sequenced before the lines in set (s+1). The main memory blocks are numbered 0 onwards. The main memory block numbered j must be mapped to any one of the cache lines from

options.html: (j mod v) * k to (j mod v) * k + (k − 1)
(j mod k) * v to (j mod k) * v + (v − 1)

solution:
Concept

In a k-way set-associative cache the lines are grouped into v sets of k lines each. A main-memory block is first assigned to exactly one set by the set-mapping rule set = (block number) mod (number of sets), i.e. s = j mod v. Within that set the block may occupy any of the k lines (that is what “k-way” means).

Because the lines are laid out one set after another — set 0’s k lines first, then set 1’s k lines, and so on — the lines belonging to set s occupy the contiguous line numbers s·k up to s·k + (k − 1).

Applying it to block j

  1. Find the set for block j: s = j mod v (the modulus is the number of sets v, not k).

  2. Find where set s starts in the line array: each earlier set contributes k lines, so set s begins at line s·k = (j mod v)·k.

  3. Set s spans k lines, so block j may map to any line from (j mod v)·k through (j mod v)·k + (k − 1).

Hence the range of cache lines is (j mod v)·k to (j mod v)·k + (k − 1).

Cross-check / why the others fail

  • The set index must use the number of sets v as the modulus; using j mod k mixes up associativity (k) with the count of sets (v).

  • The starting line of a set is the set index multiplied by k (the lines-per-set stride). A range that omits this ×k factor cannot reach the later sets’ line numbers.

  • A set contains k lines, so the span is k − 1 wide, not v − 1.

optionFeedback.html: The expression uses j mod v as its residue, multiplies that residue by k for the lower endpoint, and describes k consecutive cache-line indices.
The expression uses j mod v as its residue, takes that residue itself as the lower endpoint, and describes k consecutive cache-line indices.
The expression uses j mod k as its residue, takes that residue itself as the lower endpoint, and describes v consecutive cache-line indices.
The expression uses j mod k as its residue, multiplies that residue by v for the lower endpoint, and describes v consecutive cache-line indices.

title: Way set associative cache of KB is used in system
subject: COA
text: 4 way set associative cache of 64 KB is used in a system with 32 bits address. The 32 bits address is subdivided into TAG, INDEX and BLOCK OFFSET. No. of bits in TAG is:
solution:
Cache size is 64 KB (2^16 bytes) with 4-way associativity. Address bits are 32.

Index bits + Offset bits = log2(Cache Size) - log2(Associativity) = 16 - 2 = 14 bits.

Tag bits = Address - (Index + Offset) = 32 - 14 = 18 bits.

optionFeedback.html: This value suggests an error in calculating the number of sets or block offset. Remember to divide cache size by associativity before determining index bits.
For a 64 KB, 4-way cache, the index and offset bits sum to 14. The TAG bits are calculated as total address bits minus this sum.
This value indicates a miscalculation in the address breakdown. Recall that index bits depend on the number of sets derived from cache size and associativity.
This value implies an incorrect derivation of the index bits. Ensure you divide the total cache size by the associativity factor before calculating the number of sets.

title: Consider 4-way set associative mapping with cache block. The memory
subject: COA
text:
Consider a 4-way set associative mapping with 16 cache block. The memory block requests are in the order:

0, 255, 1, 4, 3, 8, 133, 159, 216, 129, 63, 8, 48, 32, 73, 92, 155

If LRU replacement policy is used, which cache block will be present in the Final cache?
solution:
Associativity: 4-way set associative

Total cache blocks: 16

Blocks per set: 16 / 4 = 4 (so there are 4 sets, indexed 0 to 3)

Set mapping rule: use block number mod 4 to determine the set (set = block mod 4).

Key idea: each set holds up to 4 blocks; on a hit the block becomes most recently used; on a miss, if the set is full, the least recently used block is evicted and the new block becomes most recently used.

Final contents of each set (MRU listed first, LRU last):

  • Set 0: 92 (MRU), 32, 48, 8 (LRU)

  • Set 1: 73 (MRU), 129, 133, 1 (LRU)

  • Set 2: (empty)

  • Set 3: 155 (MRU), 63, 159, 3 (LRU)

Explanation of why the listed blocks are present:

  1. Block 3 maps to set 3 (3 mod 4 = 3) and was not evicted by later accesses, so it remains in the final cache.

  2. Block 8 maps to set 0 (8 mod 4 = 0). It was re-accessed during the sequence and survived the later evictions, so it is in the final set 0.

  3. Block 129 maps to set 1 (129 mod 4 = 1) and remains in the final set 1.

  4. Block 216 mapped to set 0 but was evicted later when block 92 was inserted into set 0 under LRU, so 216 is not present.

Conclusion: The blocks from the provided choices that are present in the final cache are 3, 8, and 129. The full final cache contents (by set) are listed above for reference.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. Block 3 maps to set 3 because 3 mod 4 = 3. After processing the sequence with 4-way associativity and LRU replacement, block 3 remains in the final contents of set 3, so it is present in the final cache.

Incorrect. Block 216 maps to set 0 because 216 mod 4 = 0. It was loaded into set 0 earlier but was later the least recently used entry and was evicted when block 92 was inserted into that set under the LRU policy, so 216 is not in the final cache.

Correct. Block 8 maps to set 0 (8 mod 4 = 0). It was accessed again during the sequence which refreshed its recency, and after the subsequent insertions and evictions under LRU, block 8 remains in the final contents of set 0, so it is present in the final cache.

Correct. Block 129 maps to set 1 because 129 mod 4 = 1. It was loaded into set 1 and was not evicted by later accesses, so it remains in the final contents of that set and is present in the final cache.

title: Conflict miss occur in…….
subject: COA
text: Conflict miss occur in…….
solution:
Answer: Conflict misses can occur in both set-associative (k-way) and direct-mapped caches.

Why:

  • Direct-mapped: each memory block maps to exactly one cache line. If two blocks map to the same line they evict each other, producing conflict misses.

  • Set-associative (k-way): blocks map to a set of k lines. If more than k blocks map to the same set they compete for the k lines and conflict misses occur.

  • Fully associative: a block may be placed in any line, which eliminates conflict misses (only capacity and compulsory misses remain).

Example: If three blocks map to the same 2-way set, one block must be evicted when the third is loaded, causing a conflict miss even though other parts of the cache are free.

optionFeedback.html: Partly correct. Conflict misses can occur in set-associative (k-way) caches when more than k blocks map to the same set and compete for the available lines, causing evictions. The complete answer is that conflict misses can occur in both set-associative and direct-mapped caches.

Partly correct. In direct-mapped caches each memory block maps to a single cache line; when multiple blocks map to that same line they evict each other and produce conflict misses. The complete answer is that conflict misses can occur in both direct-mapped and set-associative caches.

Correct. Conflict misses occur in both set-associative (k-way) and direct-mapped caches because blocks can map to the same set or line and evict each other. Note that fully associative caches do not suffer from conflict misses (they can still have capacity and compulsory misses).
Incorrect. Conflict misses do occur in direct-mapped and set-associative caches, so 'none of the above' is not correct.

title: Which of the following is/are correct:
subject: COA
text: Which of the following is/are correct:

options.html: Increase in block size can reduce Compulsory miss.
Increasing disc size can reduce Conflict miss.
Increasing set lines can reduce Capacity miss
Reducing block size can impact spatial locality

solution:
Answer: The correct statements are: "Increase in block size can reduce Compulsory miss." and "Reducing block size can impact spatial locality."

  • Increase in block size can reduce Compulsory miss. Why: Compulsory (cold) misses occur on the first access to a block. A larger block (cache line) brings in more adjacent data on each miss, so fewer distinct first-time block accesses are needed when nearby addresses are subsequently used. Note: Very large blocks can increase miss penalty and reduce effective cache capacity, potentially increasing other miss types.

  • Increasing disc size can reduce Conflict miss. Assessment: This statement is incorrect as written. If the intent was to refer to increasing total cache size, that reduces capacity misses (insufficient total space). Conflict misses are reduced by increasing associativity or the number of sets so that multiple blocks that map to the same set can coexist. If "disc" literally means disk, it is not relevant to cache conflict misses.

  • Increasing set lines can reduce Capacity miss Assessment: This is incorrect. Increasing the number of lines per set (increasing associativity) primarily reduces conflict misses by allowing more blocks to map to the same set without eviction. Capacity misses are reduced by increasing the total number of blocks in the cache (i.e., larger cache size).

  • Reducing block size can impact spatial locality. Why: Smaller blocks fetch less adjacent data on a miss, so programs that rely on spatial locality may see more misses. Trade-offs: Smaller blocks can reduce miss penalty and internal fragmentation and may sometimes improve conflict behavior, so the net effect depends on access patterns.

Summary: The statements about block size reducing compulsory misses and block size affecting spatial locality are correct. The other statements mix up which cache parameter affects which miss type: total cache size affects capacity misses, and associativity (set lines) affects conflict misses.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. Compulsory (cold) misses happen the first time a block is accessed. Increasing the block (cache line) size brings in more adjacent data on each miss, so fewer first-time misses occur for nearby addresses. Note the trade-off: very large blocks can increase miss penalty and reduce effective cache capacity, which may worsen other miss types.

Incorrect. Increasing cache size (not "disc size") tends to reduce capacity misses, not conflict misses. Conflict misses are reduced by increasing associativity or the number of sets (so accesses that previously mapped to the same line can coexist). If the option meant disk size, that is unrelated to cache conflict misses.

Incorrect. Increasing the number of lines per set (increasing associativity) reduces conflict misses because fewer accesses map to the same set and evict each other. Capacity misses are reduced by increasing the total cache size (more blocks overall), not by increasing associativity alone.

Correct. Reducing block size fetches fewer contiguous bytes on a miss, so less nearby data is brought into cache; this can harm spatial locality when adjacent data is used. Also mention trade-offs: smaller blocks can reduce miss penalty and internal fragmentation and sometimes reduce conflict misses.

title: Which of the following misses can be reduced without changing
subject: COA
text:
Which of the following misses can be reduced without changing the cache size.

i. conflict miss ii. Capacity miss iii. Compulsory miss
solution:
Answer: Conflict misses and compulsory (cold) misses can be reduced without changing the total cache size.

  • Conflict misses — can be reduced by increasing associativity or using a different placement policy. These changes alter how blocks are mapped to lines but do not require increasing the total cache capacity.

  • Capacity misses — depend on the total cache capacity (the number of bytes the cache can hold). Reducing capacity misses requires increasing the total cache size or reducing the working set, so they cannot generally be reduced without changing cache size.

  • Compulsory (cold) misses — can be reduced by increasing block (line) size so each miss brings more contiguous data (exploiting spatial locality). This can be done while keeping the overall cache capacity constant by decreasing the number of lines accordingly, so compulsory misses can be reduced without increasing total cache size.

Conclusion: Conflict and compulsory misses can be reduced without changing the total cache size; capacity misses cannot.

optionFeedback.html: The selection that lists conflict miss and capacity miss is not correct. Conflict misses can be reduced without changing total cache size (for example by increasing associativity or changing the mapping). Capacity misses, however, depend on the total cache capacity and are reduced only by increasing the cache size (or by reducing the program working set), so they cannot generally be reduced without changing cache size.

The selection that lists conflict miss and compulsory miss is correct. Conflict misses can be reduced without changing total cache size by increasing associativity or using better placement policies. Compulsory (cold) misses can be reduced by increasing block (line) size to capture more spatial locality; this can be done while keeping the total cache capacity constant by reducing the number of lines. Capacity misses are not reduced without increasing total cache size.

The selection that lists conflict, capacity, and compulsory misses is not correct. While conflict and compulsory misses can be addressed without increasing total cache capacity (by changing associativity or block size respectively), capacity misses arise from the cache's limited total capacity and require increasing the cache size to reduce.

The selection that states none of the above is not correct. There is a valid way to reduce some miss types without changing total cache size: conflict misses (via higher associativity) and compulsory misses (via larger block size while keeping total cache size constant by adjusting the number of lines).

title: Consider 4-way set associative cache (initially empty) with total cache
subject: COA
text:
Consider a 4-way set associative cache (initially empty) with total 8 cache block. The main memory consists of 256 blocks and the request for memory blocks is in the following order.

0, 256, 1, 4, 3, 126, 216, 8, 92, 48, 36, 159

Which of the following memory block will not be in cache if LRU replacement policy is used?
solution:
Explanation and final cache contents:

Cache configuration: total 8 blocks, 4-way set associative => number of sets = 8 / 4 = 2 sets. Use block number modulo 2 to determine set: even blocks map to the even set, odd blocks map to the odd set.

Process the request sequence under LRU (track only set contents):

  1. Request 0 (even): load into even set => even set: [0]

  2. Request 256 (even): even set: [0, 256]

  3. Request 1 (odd): odd set: [1]

  4. Request 4 (even): even set: [0, 256, 4]

  5. Request 3 (odd): odd set: [1, 3]

  6. Request 126 (even): even set becomes full: [0, 256, 4, 126]

  7. Request 216 (even): even set full, evict LRU (0) => even set: [256, 4, 126, 216]

  8. Request 8 (even): evict LRU (256) => even set: [4, 126, 216, 8]

  9. Request 92 (even): evict LRU (4) => even set: [126, 216, 8, 92]

  10. Request 48 (even): evict LRU (126) => even set: [216, 8, 92, 48]

  11. Request 36 (even): evict LRU (216) => even set: [8, 92, 48, 36]

  12. Request 159 (odd): odd set: [1, 3, 159]

Final contents by set:

  • Even-numbered set: 8, 92, 48, 36

  • Odd-numbered set: 1, 3, 159

Therefore, the memory blocks that are not in the cache after the sequence are 4 and 126 (they were evicted by LRU replacements in the even-numbered set).

optionFeedback.html: Block 4 is not in the final cache. It maps to the set for even-numbered blocks. It was loaded into that set early, but was later evicted under LRU when newer even-numbered blocks (216, 8, 92, 48, 36) filled the four-way set and caused the least recently used entry (4) to be removed.

Block 126 is not in the final cache. It maps to the same even-numbered set as other even blocks. After it was brought into the set, subsequent even-block requests caused LRU replacements. By the time block 48 was loaded, block 126 had become the least recently used and was evicted.

Block 36 is in the final cache. It maps to the even-numbered set and was the last even block requested, so it remained in the set after the sequence finished. It was not evicted because no later even-numbered requests occurred after it was loaded.
Block 159 remains in the final cache. It maps to the odd-numbered set and that set never exceeded its four-entry capacity for odd requests in this sequence, so 159 was not evicted.

title: Consider small 2-way set-associative cache memory, consisting of four blocks.

title: Which of the following statements is/are true:
subject: COA
text: Which of the following statements is/are true:

options.html: Cache replacements (LRU, MRU, FIFO, etc. ) policy are used to improve Temporal locality of cache.
Cache replacements (LRU, MRU, FIFO, etc. ) policy are used to improve Spatial locality of cache.
While accessing a large array, a cache with improved spatial locality will perform better as compared to improved temporal locality
While executing a loop, a cache with improved spatial locality will perform better as compared to improved temporal locality

solution:
Solution: Spatial and temporal locality are concepts from computer science that describe patterns of access in memory by programs which improves cache performance.

Temporal locality refers to the tendency of a program to access the same memory location repeatedly within a short period of time. This principle is based on the observation that once a memory location is accessed, it is likely to be accessed again soon. To improve temporal locality we use cache replacement policy which suits best to our situation. Examples include:

Loop variables: When a variable is accessed inside a loop, it is likely to be accessed repeatedly as the loop iterates.

Spatial locality refers to the tendency of a program to access memory locations that are close to each other within a short period of time. This principle is based on

the observation that once a memory location is accessed, nearby memory locations are likely to be accessed soon. It can be improved by increasing size of block.

Examples include:

Array elements: Accessing one element of an array often means that nearby elements will also be accessed soon.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q62
subject: COA
text: The primary purpose of an associative cache is to
solution:
Concept

Cache misses are classified by the 3Cs model into three categories: compulsory (cold) misses that occur on a block's very first reference regardless of cache design, capacity misses that occur because the cache is too small to hold the full working set, and conflict (collision) misses that occur when multiple blocks compete for the same limited set of locations even though the cache has spare capacity elsewhere. A cache's placement policy -- how many locations a given memory block may occupy -- is exactly what determines how much conflict-miss traffic it generates.

Application

  1. In a direct-mapped cache, each memory block maps to exactly one cache line, so two blocks that alias to the same line evict each other every time both are actively used, even when many other lines sit empty -- these are conflict misses.

  2. An associative cache design (set-associative or fully associative) lets a block be placed in any of several lines within a set (or, in a fully associative cache, anywhere at all), so blocks that would collide under direct mapping can now coexist without evicting one another.

  3. Increasing the number of ways of associativity therefore relaxes the placement restriction and directly attacks conflict misses, while leaving the block's first-ever fetch (compulsory misses) and the total data volume the program touches versus the total cache size (capacity misses) unchanged.

  4. Hence the primary purpose served by adding associativity to a cache is reducing conflict misses.

Cross-check

Checking each option against the standard 3Cs classification confirms this:

  • Reduce compulsory misses -- compulsory misses are fixed by the number of distinct blocks referenced for the first time; they occur on the very first access to a block no matter how the cache is organized, so associativity cannot change their count.

  • Reduce conflict misses -- this is the miss category directly tied to the placement policy, i.e. how freely a block can be positioned, which is precisely what associativity changes.

  • Reduce capacity misses -- capacity misses are governed by total cache size relative to the working set; increasing associativity while holding total cache size fixed adds no capacity, so this class is essentially untouched.

  • Reduce write-back traffic -- write-back traffic is a consequence of the write policy (write-back vs write-through) and dirty-block eviction, not of how many locations a block may occupy.

optionFeedback.html: Compulsory misses (also called cold misses) are the misses that occur the very first time a particular memory block is referenced, before it has ever been brought into the cache.
Conflict misses (also called collision misses) are the residual category in the classic 3Cs breakdown, covering whatever misses remain after compulsory and capacity misses are accounted for.
Capacity misses occur when the working set of a program is larger than the entire cache, so blocks are evicted purely because the cache cannot hold everything the program is actively using.
Write-back traffic refers to the data transferred from cache to main memory when a modified (dirty) cache block is evicted, and its volume is governed by the cache's write policy.

title: Suppose that in memory reference there are misses in the
subject: COA
text: Suppose that in 1000 memory reference there are 40 misses in the first level cache and 20 misses in the second level cache. Assume miss penalty from the L2 cache to memory is 100 cycles the hit time of the L2 cache is 10 clock cycles. The hit time of the L1 cache is 1 clock cycle. If there are 1.5 memory references per instruction on average, what is the average stall cycle per instruction?
solution:
Step 1 — Compute miss rates:

  • L1 miss rate = 40 / 1000 = 0.04.

  • L2 local miss rate (given an L1 miss) = 20 / 40 = 0.5.

Step 2 — Compute average miss penalty per memory reference:

Use the formula: average penalty per memory reference = L1_miss_rate * (L2_hit_time + L2_local_miss_rate * memory_miss_penalty).

Plug in the numbers: 0.04 * (10 + 0.5 * 100) = 0.04 * (10 + 50) = 0.04 * 60 = 2.4 cycles per memory reference.

Step 3 — Convert to per-instruction stall cycles:

There are 1.5 memory references per instruction on average, so stall cycles per instruction = 2.4 * 1.5 = 3.6 cycles.

Answer: 3.6 cycles per instruction.

The average miss penalty per memory reference = 0.04 * (L2 hit time + L2 local miss rate * memory miss penalty) = 0.04 * (10 + 0.5 * 100) = 2.4 cycles. Multiply by 1.5 memory references per instruction: 2.4 * 1.5 = 3.6 cycles per instruction. So 3.4 cycles is not correct.

Convert to per-instruction by multiplying by 1.5 memory refs/instruction: 2.4 * 1.5 = 3.6 cycles per instruction. Therefore 3.5 cycles is not the correct result.

title: In two-level virtual memory, the memory access time for main
subject: COA
text: In a two-level virtual memory, the memory access time for main memory t1 = 1 nanosecond and the memory access time for the secondary memory t2 = 0.1 millisecond. What must be the hit ratio H (in%) such that the access efficiency is within 85% of its maximum value? (using simultaneous access)
solution:
Given: t1 = 1 ns (main memory) and t2 = 0.1 ms (secondary memory).

For simultaneous access, the average access time is tavg = H·t1 + (1−H)·t2.

The requirement "access efficiency is within 85% of its maximum value" is interpreted here as the average access time being at most 85% of the maximum access time, i.e. tavg ≤ 0.85·t2.

Set tavg = 0.85·t2 and solve for H:

0.85·t2 = H·t1 + (1−H)·t2 = t2 − H·(t2 − t1)

Rearrange: H·(t2 − t1) = t2 − 0.85·t2 = 0.15·t2

So H = 0.15·t2 / (t2 − t1).

Substitute t1 = 1×10⁻⁹ s and t2 = 1×10⁻⁴ s. Note t1/t2 = 10⁻5, so:

H = 0.15 / (1 − 1×10⁻5) ≈ 0.1500015

Therefore the required hit ratio is approximately 15.00015%, which is about 15%.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The required hit ratio is about 15%, so 10% is too low. With a 10% hit ratio, the average access time would be approximately 0.900001 × t2, which is greater than 0.85 × t2 and therefore does not meet the requirement.
Correct. Using simultaneous access, the average access time is tavg = H·t1 + (1−H)·t2. Requiring tavg ≤ 0.85·t2 and solving gives H ≈ 0.1500015, i.e. about 15%. So 15% meets the requirement.
Incorrect. A 2% hit ratio is far too small. With H = 2%, the average access time is roughly 0.98 × t2, which is well above 0.85 × t2 and does not satisfy the condition.

Not the intended answer. A 40% hit ratio would certainly make the average access time smaller than 0.85 × t2, but the question asks for the hit ratio that must be achieved (the threshold value). The minimal required hit ratio is about 15%, so 40% is higher than necessary.

title: How much speed do we gain by using the cache,
subject: COA
text: How much speed do we gain by using the cache when the cache is used 80% of the time? Assume the cache is 20 times faster than the main memory.
solution:
Concept

A cache speeds up memory access because most requests are served by the fast cache instead of the slow main memory. If a fraction h of the accesses hit the cache and the remaining (1 − h) go to main memory, the average (effective) access time is EAT = h·Tc + (1 − h)·Tm. The speed gain from using the cache is the time needed WITHOUT it divided by the time needed WITH it:

Speedup = Tm / EAT = Tm / [ h·Tc + (1 − h)·Tm ]

Applying it here

The cache is used 80% of the time, so h = 0.8; and the cache is 20 times faster than main memory, so Tm = 20·Tc. Take Tc = 1 unit, which makes Tm = 20 units.

  1. Effective access time: EAT = 0.8 × 1 + 0.2 × 20.

  2. EAT = 0.8 + 4 = 4.8 units.

  3. Speed gain = Tm / EAT = 20 / 4.8.

  4. Speed gain = 4.166… ≈ 4.16.

Cross-check

The maximum speed gain at an 80% hit ratio happens when the cache is infinitely fast (Tc → 0), and it equals 1 / (1 − h) = 1 / 0.2 = 5. The answer 4.16 lies just under this ceiling of 5, so it is consistent. Any value above 5 is impossible at this hit ratio, and a value close to 2 would require the cache to be only about 2–3 times faster than main memory, not 20 times.

optionFeedback.html: This is the speed gain for the classic textbook case of a cache that is 10 times faster and is used 90% of the time, where 1 / (0.9×0.1 + 0.1) ≈ 5.26. Those are not the figures in this problem — here the cache is used 80% of the time and is 20 times faster — so that parameter set does not apply.

This value corresponds to assuming the cache is only about 2 to 3 times faster than main memory. The problem states a 20-times speed difference, so this uses the wrong speed ratio between cache and main memory.

With h = 0.8 and the cache 20 times faster than main memory (Tm = 20·Tc), the effective access time is 0.8×1 + 0.2×20 = 4.8 cache-time units, so the speed gain is 20 ÷ 4.8 = 4.16. This is exactly what the effective-access-time formula gives for the stated hit ratio and speed difference.

This value cannot be produced by the effective-access-time formula with an 80% hit ratio and a 20-times speed difference; it usually comes from an arithmetic slip such as swapping the hit and miss weights. Set up the weighted average again, using h = 0.8 for the fast cache and (1 − h) for the slow main memory.

title: Consider MHz CPU based system. What is the number of
subject: COA
text: Consider a 33 MHz CPU based system. What is the number of wait states required if it is interfaced with a 60 ns memory? Assume a maximum of 10 ns delay for additional circuitry like buffering and decoding.
solution:
Concept: When a CPU's clock cycle is shorter than the time a memory device needs to respond, the memory interface must insert idle clock cycles — wait states — so the total elapsed time covers the memory's actual response time. If T is the CPU clock period and A is the total time the interface needs (raw memory access time plus any buffering/decoding delay), the number of whole clock cycles required is N = ceil(A / T). Because the first of those cycles is the base memory-access cycle itself, the number of wait states inserted equals (N − 1), not N.

Applying this to the given system:

  1. Clock period: T = 1 / f = 1 / 33 MHz ≈ 30.3 ns.

  2. Total time the interface needs: A = memory access time + circuitry delay = 60 ns + 10 ns = 70 ns.

  3. Clock cycles required: N = ceil(A / T) = ceil(70 / 30.3) = ceil(2.31) = 3 cycles.

  4. Wait states = N − 1 = 3 − 1 = 2.

Cross-check: With 2 wait states (3 total cycles), the interface allows 3 × 30.3 ns ≈ 90.9 ns — enough to cover the 70 ns requirement. With only 1 wait state (2 total cycles), it allows just 2 × 30.3 ns ≈ 60.6 ns, short of the 70 ns needed. So 2 wait states is the minimum count that satisfies the timing requirement, confirming the value obtained above. (Note: rounding 70/30.3 up to 3 gives the TOTAL number of clock cycles needed — the wait states are the cycles ADDED to the base cycle, i.e. 3 − 1 = 2, not 3.)

optionFeedback.html: The corresponding access window is 1 × 30.3 ns ≈ 30.3 ns.
The corresponding access window is 2 × 30.3 ns ≈ 60.6 ns.
The corresponding access window is 3 × 30.3 ns ≈ 90.9 ns.
The corresponding access window is 4 × 30.3 ns ≈ 121.2 ns.

title: The minimum time delay between the initiation of two independent
subject: COA
text: The minimum time delay between the initiation of two independent memory operations is called
solution: The minimum time delay between the initiation of two independent memory operations is known as cycle time. While access time refers to the total duration from requesting data to its availability, cycle time specifically defines the interval required between starting one memory operation and starting another. This ensures the memory controller can handle successive requests without conflict.

optionFeedback.html: Access time measures the delay from request to data availability, not the interval between successive operations.
Cycle time defines the minimum interval between initiating two independent memory operations.
Rotational time applies to disk drives where the platter must spin, not to general memory operation intervals.
Latency refers to the delay before data is available, not necessarily the minimum interval between starting two separate operations.

title: Cache memory needs an access time of ns and main
subject: COA
text: A cache memory needs an access time of 30 ns and main memory 150 ns, what is the average access time of CPU (assume hit ratio = 80%)?
solution:
Concept — In a two-level memory hierarchy the processor always looks in the fast level (the cache) first and turns to the slow level (main memory) only when the block it needs is not there. The effective, or average, access time is therefore the fast-level time that every reference pays, plus the slow-level time that only the missing fraction of references pays. Writing H for the hit ratio, Tc for the cache access time and Tm for the main-memory access time, this sequential look-up model reads Tavg = H × Tc + (1 − H) × (Tc + Tm).

Application — substitute the quantities the stem supplies.

  1. Given data: Tc = 30 ns, Tm = 150 ns and H = 80% = 0.8, so the miss ratio is 1 − H = 0.2.

  2. Hit path: a fraction 0.8 of all references is served by the cache alone at 30 ns each, contributing 0.8 × 30 = 24 ns to the average.

  3. Miss path: the remaining fraction 0.2 first probes the cache (30 ns) and then fetches the block from main memory (150 ns), i.e. 30 + 150 = 180 ns each, contributing 0.2 × 180 = 36 ns.

  4. Add the two contributions: Tavg = 24 + 36 = 60 ns.

Cross-check — the same model rearranges to Tavg = Tc + (1 − H) × Tm = 30 + 0.2 × 150 = 30 + 30 = 60 ns, which agrees. The average must also fall between 30 ns (were every reference to hit) and 180 ns (were every reference to miss), and 60 ns sits close to the fast end, exactly where a high 80% hit ratio should place it.

A note on conventions — some texts assume simultaneous (parallel) look-up, in which the cache and main memory are searched at the same time, so a miss pays only the 150 ns main-memory access instead of the cache probe followed by the memory access; that model gives Tavg = H × Tc + (1 − H) × Tm = 0.8 × 30 + 0.2 × 150 = 54 ns. The value 54 ns is not among the four values printed on this paper, and the official ISRO answer key for the 2017 Computer Science examination marks 60 ns, so this item is set on the sequential look-up model.

optionFeedback.html: A figure of 60 ns splits into the 30 ns cache probe, which every reference pays, plus 30 ns of extra delay attributed to the references that continue on to main memory.
A figure of 30 ns splits into the 30 ns cache probe, which every reference pays, plus no extra delay attributed to the references that continue on to main memory.
A figure of 150 ns is a full main-memory access charged on every reference, with no separate cache probe and no split between references that stop at the cache and those that continue on.
A figure of 70 ns splits into the 30 ns cache probe, which every reference pays, plus 40 ns of extra delay attributed to the references that continue on to main memory.

title: Particular parallel program computation requires sec when executed on single
subject: COA
text: A particular parallel program computation requires 100 sec when executed on a single processor. If 40% of this computation is inherently sequential (i.e. will not benefit from additional processors), then theoretically best possible elapsed times of this program running with 2 and 4 processors, respectively, are
solution: To determine the theoretical best possible elapsed times, we apply Amdahl's Law. The formula for execution time with N processors is T_N = T_1 * (S + P/N), where T_1 is the single-processor time, S is the sequential fraction, and P is the parallelizable fraction. Given T_1 = 100 sec, S = 0.4 (40%), and P = 0.6 (60%). For N=2 processors: T_2 = 100 * (0.4 + 0.6/2) = 100 * (0.4 + 0.3) = 70 seconds. For N=4 processors: T_4 = 100 * (0.4 + 0.6/4) = 100 * (0.4 + 0.15) = 55 seconds. Thus, the elapsed times are 70 sec and 55 sec respectively.

optionFeedback.html: This calculation does not account for the fixed sequential portion of the workload.
This option considers only the parallelizable portion, failing to include the time for the sequential part.
This option ignores the 40% sequential portion that cannot be parallelized.

Calculate using Amdahl's Law. Sequential portion is 40 seconds. Parallelizable portion is 60 seconds. For 2 processors, parallel time halves to 30s (Total 70s). For 4 processors, parallel time quarters to 15s (Total 55s).

text: Consider a CPU that has a clock rate of 100 MHz with a single level of cache. CPI without any cache miss is 1.2. There are 40% arithmetic instructions, 30% load/store operations, 30% control instructions. Assume the cache miss rate of 10% and miss penalty of 6 clock cycles. The speed up of the ideal memory without cache miss when compared with the cache miss _______?
solution:
Given:

CPI (ideal) = 1.2

Instruction mix:

Arithmetic = 40%

Load/Store = 30%

Control = 30%

Miss rate = 10%

Miss penalty = 6 cycles

Let total number of instructions = X.

Ideal execution time (no cache miss):

= 1.2X

Only load/store instructions can cause cache miss.

Number of load/store instructions = 0.3X

Number of cache misses:

= 0.1 × 0.3X

= 0.03X

Extra cycles due to cache misses:

= 0.03X × 6

= 0.18X

Execution time with cache misses:

= 1.2X + 0.18X

= 1.38X

Speedup of ideal memory over cache-miss case:

= 1.38X / 1.2X

= 1.15

Final Answer = 1.15

title: In two-level memory, the average access time without level is
subject: COA
text: In a two-level memory, the average access time without level 1 is 180 ns and with level 1 the average access time is 60 ns. Calculate the miss ratio if level 1 access time is 45 ns.
solution:
Let h be the hit ratio (probability of finding the data in level 1).

Equation: h*45 + (1-h)*180 = 60

  • Set up the equation for average access time: h*45 + (1-h)*180 = 60.

  • Expand and combine like terms: 45h + 180 - 180h = 60 → -135h + 180 = 60 → 135h = 120.

  • Solve for h: h = 120/135 = 8/9 ≈ 0.8889.

  • Miss ratio = 1 - h = 1/9 ≈ 0.1111, which rounds to 0.11.

Answer: The miss ratio is 0.11 (rounded to two decimal places).

title: If memory access takes ns with cache and ns with
subject: COA
text: The average memory access time is 20 ns when a cache is used, and 110 ns when it is not used. If the cache itself has an access time of 10 ns, what is the cache hit ratio?
solution:
Concept

The average memory access time (AMAT) in a cache-based system is AMAT = h × Tcache + (1 − h) × Tmemory, where h is the cache hit ratio, Tcache is the access time on a cache hit, and Tmemory is the total access time when a request is served directly from main memory without the cache (a miss) — these are alternative, non-additive routes to the data, not a serial cache-then-memory lookup.

Application

  1. Given: AMAT = 20 ns, Tcache = 10 ns, Tmemory = 110 ns.

  2. Write the AMAT equation: 20 = h × 10 + (1 − h) × 110.

  3. Expand the right side: 20 = 10h + 110 − 110h.

  4. Combine like terms: 20 = 110 − 100h.

  5. Solve for h: 100h = 90, so h = 0.9.

  6. Convert to a percentage: h = 90%.

Cross-check

Substitute h = 0.9 back into the AMAT formula: 0.9 × 10 + 0.1 × 110 = 9 + 11 = 20 ns, which matches the given average access time exactly, confirming the hit ratio is 90%.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect: substituting a hit ratio of 93% into the average-access-time equation gives 0.93 × 10 + 0.07 × 110 = 17 ns, not the required 20 ns — this ratio is too high for the given access times.
Correct: solving the average-access-time equation 20 = 10h + 110(1 − h) gives h = 0.9. Substituting back, 0.9 × 10 + 0.1 × 110 = 20 ns, exactly matching the given average.
Incorrect: substituting a hit ratio of 88% gives 0.88 × 10 + 0.12 × 110 = 22 ns, higher than the required 20 ns — this ratio is too low.
Incorrect: substituting a hit ratio of 87% gives 0.87 × 10 + 0.13 × 110 = 23 ns, higher than the required 20 ns — this ratio is too low.

title: Which of the following relationships holds for non-random-access memory, where
subject: COA
text: Which of the following relationships holds for non-random-access memory, where Tₙ = average time to read or write n bits, Tₐ = average access time, n = number of bits and r = transfer rate in bits per second?
solution: The correct answer is B. For non-random-access memory (like magnetic disks or tapes), the total average time to read or write n bits (Tn) is the sum of the average access time (Ta) required to position the head, and the transfer time, which is n/r (number of bits divided by the transfer rate). Thus, Tn = Ta + n/r.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. It incorrectly states that the average access time (Ta) is the sum of total time and transfer time, which reverses the logical relationship.
Correct. It accurately defines the formula where total time (Tn) incorporates both the initial positioning delay (Ta) and the data stream transmission time (n/r).
Incorrect. The expression uses r/n for transfer time, which is dimensionally incorrect. Transfer time must be bits / (bits/second) = seconds.
Incorrect. While it places Tn on the left side, it uses the inverted and mathematically incorrect transfer time ratio r/n instead of n/r.

text: How many address lines are needed to address each memory location in a 2048 × 4 memory chip?
solution: The number of address lines depends on the total number of memory locations, not the data width. For 2048 locations, we solve $2^n = 2048$. Since $2^{11} = 2048$, 11 address lines are needed.

subject: COA
text: Assume that for a certain processor, a read request takes 50 ns on a cache miss and 5 ns on a cache hit. Suppose while running a program, it was observed that 80% of the processor’s read requests result in cache hit. The average read access time in nanoseconds is —
solution: Average time = (hit_fraction × hit_time) + (miss_fraction × miss_time) Hit fraction = 0.8, Miss fraction = 0.2 Average = 0.8×5 + 0.2×50 = 4 + 10 = 14 ns

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Compute the weighted average using hit and miss fractions: average = (hit_fraction × hit_time) + (miss_fraction × miss_time) = 0.8 × 5 + 0.2 × 50 = 4 + 10 = 14 ns. The value 10 misses the full contribution from misses or contains an arithmetic mistake.
Correct. Use the weighted average: hit contribution = 0.8 × 5 = 4 ns; miss contribution = 0.2 × 50 = 10 ns; total average = 4 + 10 = 14 ns.
Incorrect. The value 4 equals only the hit contribution (0.8 × 5 = 4). You must also include the miss contribution: 0.2 × 50 = 10. Adding both gives 14 ns.
Incorrect. Likely an arithmetic slip: hit contribution is 0.8 × 5 = 4 ns and miss contribution is 0.2 × 50 = 10 ns, so the correct total is 14 ns, not 12 ns.

title: Consider main memory system that consist of memory modules attach
subject: COA
text: Consider a main memory system that consist of 6 memory modules attach to the system bus. Which is one word wide. When a write request is made the bus occupy for 100ns by the data, control and address signals. During the same 100ns and 700ns thereafter, the address memory execute one cycle accepting and storing the data. The internal operations of different memory modules may overlap in time but only one request can be on bus at a time. The maximum number of stores that can be initiated in 1 millisecond ________________
solution:
Answer: 7500 stores in 1 ms.

Explanation:

  • Bus constraint: Each write occupies the bus for 100 ns, so the bus can initiate at most 1,000,000 ns / 100 ns = 10,000 write starts in 1 ms.

  • Module constraint: Each memory module requires 100 ns on the bus plus 700 ns internal, i.e. 800 ns total before it can accept another write. So each module can start 1,000,000 ns / 800 ns = 1250 writes in 1 ms. For 6 modules that gives 6 × 1250 = 7500 writes in 1 ms.

  • Overall limit: The maximum number of stores is the smaller of the bus-limited rate and the module-limited rate, i.e. min(10,000, 7,500) = 7,500 stores in 1 ms.

title: For multi-processor architecture, In which protocol write transaction is forwarded
subject: COA
text: For a multi-processor architecture, In which protocol a write transaction is forwarded to only those processors that are known to possess a copy of newly altered cache line ?
solution: In cache coherence protocols, snoopy bus protocols broadcast write transactions to all processors on the shared bus. In contrast, directory-based protocols maintain a central directory that tracks which caches hold copies of specific cache lines. This allows the system to forward write transactions only to those processors known to possess a copy, reducing unnecessary bus traffic.

optionFeedback.html: Snoopy bus protocols broadcast updates to all processors, not just those holding a copy.
This is a broad category of protocols, not the specific mechanism for selective forwarding.

Directory-based protocols maintain a central directory tracking cache line ownership. This allows write transactions to be forwarded selectively only to processors holding the specific data, minimizing unnecessary bus traffic compared to broadcast-based methods.
A valid protocol matching this description exists, making 'None of the above' incorrect.

title: Which of the following is an efficient method of cache
subject: COA
text: In a shared-bus multiprocessor, which of the following is an efficient cache-coherence updating method?
solution:
Concept. In a shared-bus multiprocessor, several caches may hold copies of the same memory block. A cache-coherence (cache-updating) mechanism must keep every cached copy consistent whenever one processor writes. The efficient class of techniques is bus snooping: a write appears as a transaction on the shared bus, every cache controller observes (snoops) that transaction, and only the controllers that actually hold the affected block act on it — the rest simply ignore it.

Application. The snoopy-write method applies exactly this principle. When a processor writes to a shared block, the write is seen on the bus by all cache controllers, but only those caches that currently hold that block update (or invalidate) their copy; caches without the block do nothing. Coherence is therefore maintained by selective action on the shared-bus signal, with very little extra work — this is the efficient cache-updating method.

Contrast with the other choices.

Method

What it actually does

Snoopy writes

Every controller observes the write on the shared bus, but only the caches holding the affected block update or invalidate their copy, keeping shared copies coherent with little extra work.

Write through

A write policy: sends every write straight to main memory; it sets when memory is updated, not how separate caches stay coherent, and it adds memory traffic.

Buffered write

Holds write data in a temporary buffer to hide latency and cut stalls; performs no coherence update of other caches.

Write within

Not a recognised cache-updating or coherence technique; no such standard method exists.

Cross-check. The snoopy-write method is the one choice here that actually reconciles shared cached copies — each controller watches the bus and the holders of the block update or invalidate it — whereas write-through and buffered write are write-handling policies and 'write within' is not a real method, so snooping is the efficient cache-updating method.

optionFeedback.html: The snoopy-write method denotes bus-snooping control; its operational effect is that a controller observes a write and updates or invalidates its local copy only when it holds the addressed block.
Write-through denotes a memory-update policy; its operational effect is that each processor write is propagated to main memory immediately.
Write within has no standardized definition in cache architecture; consequently, it specifies no memory-update action or cache-state transition.
Buffered write denotes a latency-hiding technique; its operational effect is that outgoing data waits in a temporary queue while the processor continues.

solution:
Concept: In processor-peripheral interfacing, a status bit and a control bit are distinguished by which side originates the information carried in that bit and which side only consults it. A status bit reports a device condition that only the peripheral itself knows (such as ready/busy), so the peripheral is the one that writes it and the CPU is the one that reads it. A control (command) bit carries an instruction that only the CPU decides, so the CPU is the one that writes it and the peripheral is the one that reads (acts on) it. For each of these two bit types, the writer and the reader sit on opposite sides of the interface.

Application: Available reproductions of the 2007 paper print “read bit,” but that is not the standard name for the device-status flag described by the choices; “ready bit” is the intended term and is used in the corrected stem. A ready bit reports a condition generated by the device. Therefore the peripheral updates the field and the CPU observes it, so the completion “by CPU and written by the peripheral” follows the status-bit access pattern.

Distinguishing the other completions:

  • "read and written by CPU" places both the read and the write action on the CPU side. Under the status/control distinction above, that pairing fits neither pattern: it is not a status bit (whose write side is the peripheral) and not a control bit (whose read side is the peripheral), since the peripheral has no role in this pairing at all.

  • "read and written by peripheral" places both actions on the peripheral side. That pairing likewise fits neither pattern: it is not a status bit (whose read side is the CPU) and not a control bit (whose write side is the CPU), since the CPU has no role in this pairing at all.

  • "read by peripheral and written by CPU" does split the roles across the two sides, but it matches the control-bit pattern instead (the CPU writes the command, the peripheral reads it) -- the opposite pairing from the ready bit the stem describes.

Cross-check: Cross-check with a familiar example: a device-busy or device-ready flag in a UART or printer status register is asserted by the controller hardware and polled (read) by the CPU's driver loop -- confirming the CPU-reads / peripheral-writes direction for a ready bit.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q71
subject: COA
text: Asynchronous buses rely on handshaking primarily because
solution:
Concept

An asynchronous bus has no shared clock between the bus master and the connected devices. Instead, the transfer is coordinated through explicit control lines — a request signal from the master and an acknowledge/ready signal from the target — and the transfer completes only once this signal exchange, or "handshake", is complete. This protocol exists because different devices on the same bus can take a different, and sometimes non-deterministic, amount of time to respond to a request.

Application

  1. The bus master asserts a request line to begin a transfer with a target device.

  2. The target device takes however long it internally needs — a duration that can differ from one device to another and even from one transfer to the next on the same device — before it can supply or accept the data.

  3. Once ready, the target asserts an acknowledge/ready line back to the master.

  4. Only after observing this acknowledge signal does the master latch the data or start the next step of the transfer.

  5. Because completion is signalled explicitly rather than assumed after a fixed number of clock cycles, the protocol works correctly no matter how long any individual device takes to respond.

Cross-check

  • A basic, fixed-timing synchronous bus assumes every transfer completes within a fixed, pre-agreed number of clock cycles referenced to a shared clock; more elaborate synchronous designs add wait-state cycles for slower devices, but these too are still sampled relative to that shared clock. An asynchronous bus, in contrast, has no shared clock at all — timing is governed purely by the request/acknowledge signal exchange itself, which is what lets any device's response time be genuinely unpredictable without breaking the protocol.

  • Clock skew — the difference in arrival time of the same clock edge at different points in a circuit — is a synchronous-design timing-margin issue handled through clock-tree design, unrelated to whether a bus uses handshaking.

  • Cache-coherence mechanisms keep cache and memory contents consistent, a memory-hierarchy concern separate from bus-transfer completion signalling.

  • Since the mechanism exists to accommodate devices whose response time is not fixed or guaranteed in advance, this confirms that handshaking is used because devices have unpredictable response time.

optionFeedback.html: Clock skew refers to the difference in arrival time of the same clock edge at different points in a circuit; the larger this difference is relative to the clock period, the smaller the safe margin left for reliably capturing data within a single cycle.

A cache controller keeps the multiple cached copies of a shared data item consistent with one another and with main memory, applying a coherence protocol such as snooping or a directory-based scheme whenever those copies are read or written.

A constant access time means a device responds within the same fixed time interval on every transfer, which lets a system relying on this property know in advance exactly when each response will arrive.

Peripheral devices attached to a bus can each take a different amount of time to respond to a request, and that time can vary from one transfer to the next even for the same device, depending on the device's internal state and the specific operation being performed.

title: Consider an interrupt processing takes about and the IO device

text: A system uses interrupt-driven I/O. The device transfers data continuously at 10 kB/s (take 1 kB = 103 bytes) and interrupts the CPU once per byte. For each byte, interrupt processing takes 50 µs and the ISR spends a further 10 µs transferring the byte. What percentage of CPU time is consumed by servicing this device?
solution:
Concept

For an interrupt-driven device, CPU utilization equals the interrupt rate multiplied by the CPU service time per interrupt. Converting the occupied CPU time in each second to a percentage gives utilization = (occupied CPU time / 1 s) × 100.

Application

  1. The interrupt rate is 10 kB/s × 103 bytes/kB = 10,000 interrupts/s because there is one interrupt per byte.

  2. The CPU service time per byte is 50 µs + 10 µs = 60 µs.

  3. CPU time occupied in one second is 10,000 × 60 µs = 600,000 µs = 0.6 s.

  4. Therefore, the percentage of CPU time consumed is (0.6 s / 1 s) × 100 = 60%.

Cross-check

The maximum service rate at 60 µs per byte is 1/(60 µs) ≈ 16,666.67 bytes/s. The actual rate is 10,000/16,666.67 = 0.60 of this capacity, which confirms 60%.

title: Consider system employing interrupt driven input/output for particular device that

title: In vectored interrupt

The interrupting source supplies the branch information to the processor
The branch address is obtained from a register in the processor

solution:
Concept

An interrupt vector is a value associated with an interrupt source that identifies the handler to execute.

In a vectored interrupt system, the processor receives the vector during interrupt acknowledgement and uses it to select the corresponding interrupt service routine (ISR).

Application

Here the interrupting source supplies the branch information, namely the vector, to the processor. The processor uses that vector to locate the corresponding ISR, so it does not need to poll every possible source.

Contrast

Authoritative device-driver documentation distinguishes vectored devices by their supply of an interrupt vector during interrupt acknowledgement; polled devices do not supply one.

solution:
Answer: Stack overflow → Internal interrupt; Timer → External interrupt; Invalid opcode → Machine check interrupt; Superior call → Software interrupt.

  • Stack overflow is an internal interrupt (exception) because it arises from erroneous program execution (e.g., excessive recursion or stack growth) and is handled by the processor as an exception.

  • Timer is an external interrupt since it is generated asynchronously by a hardware timer device outside the CPU.

  • Invalid opcode is detected by the CPU during instruction decode/execution and is treated as a machine-level fault in many architectures; such faults are classed as machine check interrupts.

  • Superior (supervisor) call is a software-generated interrupt used by a program to request privileged OS services, so it is a software interrupt.

Therefore the correct classification is: Stack overflow → Internal interrupt; Timer → External interrupt; Invalid opcode → Machine check interrupt; Superior call → Software interrupt.

optionFeedback.html: This mapping is incorrect. Stack overflow is an internal interrupt (an exception caused by program execution), not a software interrupt. Timer interrupts come from hardware devices and are external interrupts, not internal. Invalid opcode is detected by the processor as an exception or machine-level fault, not an external interrupt. A superior (supervisor) call is a software-generated interrupt used to request OS services, not a machine check.

This mapping has partly correct and partly incorrect pairs. It correctly assigns stack overflow to an internal interrupt and timer to an external interrupt. However, assigning invalid opcode to a software interrupt is incorrect—invalid opcode is a fault detected by the CPU (an exception or machine-level fault). Assigning superior (supervisor) call to a machine check is incorrect because a supervisor call is a deliberate software interrupt used for system calls.

This mapping is incorrect. It assigns stack overflow to a software interrupt and timer to an internal interrupt, both of which are wrong: stack overflow is an internal exception, and timer interrupts are external hardware interrupts. It also assigns superior (supervisor) call to an external interrupt, but a supervisor call is a software-generated interrupt. While it maps invalid opcode to a machine check (which is consistent with treating illegal instructions as hardware-detected faults in some architectures), the other pairings are incorrect.

Correct. Stack overflow is an internal interrupt (an exception caused by program execution), timer interrupts are external interrupts generated by hardware timers, invalid opcode is treated as a machine-level fault detected by the CPU (a machine check in many architectures), and a superior (supervisor) call is a software-generated interrupt used to request OS services.

title: Statement: The DMA technique is more efficient than the interrupt
subject: COA
text:
Statement: The DMA technique is more efficient than the interrupt driven technique for high volume I/O data transfer.
Reason : The DMA technique does not make use of the interrupt mechanism

options.html: Statement is true but Reason is false
Statement is false but Reason is true
Statement is true and Reason is true and Reason is correct explanation for Statement
Both Statement and Reason are true but Reason is not correct explanation for Statement

solution:
Answer: The statement is true, but the original reason is misstated.

  • How DMA works: A DMA controller transfers blocks of data directly between an I/O device and main memory with little CPU involvement.

  • Interrupt-driven I/O: The CPU is interrupted for each byte or word transferred, causing high CPU overhead for high-volume transfers.

  • Interrupts and DMA: DMA typically generates an interrupt only when a block transfer completes or on error. It does not eliminate interrupts entirely, but it greatly reduces their frequency compared with interrupt-driven I/O.

Conclusion: DMA is more efficient for high-volume I/O because it minimizes CPU involvement and the number of interrupts required, reducing overhead compared to interrupt-driven techniques.

optionFeedback.html: The statement is correct: DMA is more efficient than interrupt-driven I/O for high-volume data transfers because it moves large blocks of data directly between device and memory with minimal CPU intervention. The reason given is incorrect as written: DMA does make limited use of interrupts to signal transfer completion or errors. The key difference is that interrupt-driven I/O can generate an interrupt for each byte/word, while DMA generates far fewer interrupts.

This choice claims the statement is false and the reason is true, but that is incorrect. The statement is true: DMA is more efficient for high-volume transfers. The reason as stated is false because DMA does use interrupts to indicate completion or errors, although it avoids per-byte interrupts. Clarify that DMA reduces CPU overhead by handling transfers autonomously and only interrupts on completion.

Correct. DMA is more efficient for high-volume I/O because it transfers blocks of data directly between memory and the I/O device with minimal CPU intervention. The reason needs a small clarification: DMA typically uses interrupts only to signal completion or errors, not for every data unit, which is why it avoids the heavy interrupt overhead of interrupt-driven I/O.

This choice asserts both are true but that the reason is not the correct explanation. In reality the reason given is incorrect: DMA does use interrupts to signal completion or errors. The statement is true, but the reason as stated is false, so this choice is incorrect. Emphasize that DMA's efficiency comes from reduced CPU involvement and far fewer interrupts, not from a total absence of interrupts.

title: The ability to temporarily halt the CPU and use this
subject: COA

solution: The correct concept is Cycle Stealing. In this process, the DMA controller temporarily halts CPU execution to gain control of system buses for data transfer. optionFeedback.html: DMA allows peripherals to access memory directly without CPU intervention, but the specific action of halting the CPU temporarily for bus transfers describes a distinct technique.

title: In DMA transfer scheme, the transfer scheme other than burst
subject: COA
text: In DMA transfer scheme, the transfer scheme other than burst mode is
solution: Direct Memory Access (DMA) transfer schemes are primarily categorized into Burst Mode and Cycle Stealing Mode. While Burst Mode allows the DMA controller to transfer a block of data continuously, Cycle Stealing Mode transfers data one word at a time by stealing bus cycles. Thus, the scheme other than burst mode is Cycle Stealing Mode.

This term is incomplete and does not accurately describe the standard DMA transfer mode.
Cycle stealing allows the DMA controller to take control of the bus for single data transfers.

title: Two control signals in microprocessor which are related to Direct
subject: COA
text: Two control signals in microprocessor which are related to Direct Memory Access (DMA) are
solution: Direct Memory Access (DMA) allows peripheral devices to transfer data directly to memory without CPU intervention. To achieve this, the DMA controller asserts the HOLD signal to request control of the system bus. The microprocessor responds by asserting the HLDA (Hold Acknowledge) signal, indicating it has relinquished bus control. Therefore, HOLD and HLDA are the specific control signals associated with DMA operations.

optionFeedback.html: INTR and INTA are interrupt control signals used for handling hardware interrupts, not specifically for Direct Memory Access bus arbitration.

title: Processor is fetching instructions at the rate of MIPS. DMA
subject: COA
text: A processor fetches instructions at a rate of 1 MIPS. A DMA module transfers 8-bit characters to RAM from a device transmitting at 9600 bps. Assume that each instruction fetch occupies one memory cycle and that cycle stealing uses one equal-duration memory cycle per transferred character. How much processor time is lost during each second of operation?
solution:
Concept

In cycle-stealing DMA, the processor pauses for one memory cycle whenever the DMA controller transfers one data unit. When an instruction fetch and a DMA transfer occupy equal-duration memory cycles, processor time lost per second equals DMA transfers per second multiplied by the duration of one instruction-fetch cycle.

Application

  1. Convert the device rate to characters per second: 9600 bits/s ÷ 8 bits/character = 1200 characters/s.

  2. With one stolen memory cycle per character, DMA takes 1200 processor cycles during each second.

  3. At 1 MIPS, one million instruction fetches take one second. Under the stated equal-cycle assumption, one memory cycle therefore takes 1 microsecond.

  4. The total stolen time is 1200 × 1 microsecond = 1200 microseconds = 1.2 ms per second.

Cross-check

The stolen fraction is 1200 ÷ 1,000,000 = 0.0012 = 0.12%. Taking 0.12% of one second again gives 0.0012 s = 1.2 ms.

Therefore, the processor loses 1.2 ms of execution time during each second of operation.

A duration of 4.8 ms equals 4,800 microseconds, which is 0.48% of a one-second interval.
A duration of 2.4 ms equals 2,400 microseconds, which is 0.24% of a one-second interval.
A duration of 1.2 ms equals 1,200 microseconds, which is 0.12% of a one-second interval.

title: The term cycle stealing is used in context of:
subject: COA
text: The term cycle stealing is used in context of:
solution:
Cycle Stealing is a method used in Direct Memory Access (DMA) data transfer. In this mode, the DMA controller "steals" or borrows a bus cycle from the CPU to transfer a single word of data.

  • Since the CPU and DMA controller share the same system bus, the DMA controller requests the CPU to pause its bus activity for one clock cycle.

  • The CPU suspends its operation for that specific cycle, allowing the DMA to transfer data directly between the I/O device and memory.

  • This is highly efficient because the CPU doesn't stop entirely; it just slows down slightly while data is transferred in the background.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Here, the CPU is actively involved in the transfer process by executing an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR). It doesn't involve "stealing" cycles.
Incorrect. In polling, the CPU constantly checks the status of an I/O device, wasting many CPU cycles. It is the opposite of the efficiency seen in cycle stealing.
Correct. Cycle stealing is a specific DMA mode where the controller takes control of the bus for one cycle at a time.
Incorrect. This is a non-standard technical term and is not related to standard I/O data transfer methods.

title: During DMA transfer, DMA controller transfers data
subject: COA
text: During DMA transfer, the DMA controller transfers data ______.

options.html: directly between the I/O module and main memory

solution:
Concept

Direct Memory Access (DMA) is a bus-mastering mechanism in which a DMA controller moves a block of data between an I/O interface and main memory. The CPU configures the transfer and is notified when it finishes, but it does not carry each data word.

Application

Here, the blank asks for the two endpoints used during the transfer phase. The DMA controller obtains bus control, reads from one endpoint, and writes to the other, so the data path is between the I/O module and main memory.

Contrast and cross-check

  • CPU to memory describes the processor acting as the source of a store or copy operation.

  • Memory to CPU describes a processor load in which the CPU receives a value.

  • Memory and processor registers describes instruction-level load/store movement inside the processor–memory path.

  • I/O module and main memory describes the DMA block-transfer path while the CPU is limited to setup and completion handling.

Result

Therefore, the DMA controller transfers data directly between the I/O module and main memory.

Memory-to-CPU movement is a processor load or read, so the CPU receives data into its execution state in this path.
Memory-to-register movement is an instruction-level load/store exchange between main memory and processor registers.

title: What is the main characteristic of Cycle Stealing in Direct
subject: COA
text: What is the main characteristic of Cycle Stealing in Direct Memory Access?

options.html: The DMA controller temporarily borrows the system bus for a single cycle during CPU idle time.
The CPU and DMA controller execute simultaneously without interference.
The CPU and DMA controller share the same clock cycle for data transfer.
The DMA controller halts the CPU until the entire data transfer is completed.

solution:
In Cycle Stealing, the I/O device operates much slower than the memory or the CPU. It prepares one byte or word of data at a time. The process follows a highly fast cycle:

The Request: The DMAC senses that one word of data is ready for transfer and issues a bus request (BR) to the CPU.

The Grant: The CPU finishes its current clock cycle, releases control of the buses, and replies with a bus grant (BG).

The Theft: The DMAC "steals" exactly one bus cycle to transfer that single word directly to memory.

The Release: The DMAC immediately drops the bus request, handing control right back to the CPU.

optionFeedback.html: This perfectly defines the mechanism of Cycle Stealing. Instead of taking control of the system bus for a prolonged duration, the DMA controller pauses the CPU for just one clock cycle (or takes advantage of a cycle where the CPU is not utilizing the buses) to transfer a single word of data. It then immediately hands the bus back to the CPU, minimizing CPU idling.

The CPU and the DMA controller share the exact same physical system buses (Address, Data, and Control lines). Since two hardware units cannot drive the same buses at the exact same moment without causing electrical conflicts, they cannot execute bus-reliant operations simultaneously without interference.

They do not share or merge a single clock cycle to transfer data together. Rather, they alternate ownership of the clock cycles. During a "stolen" cycle, the DMA controller owns the bus entirely, while the CPU operations that require bus access are temporarily frozen.

This statement describes Burst Mode (or Block Transfer Mode) DMA, not Cycle Stealing. In Burst Mode, the DMA controller continuous-fires a massive block of data and locks the CPU completely out of the system bus until the entire transfer finishes.

title: Consider file consisting of records each record is of size
subject: COA
text: Consider a file consisting of 70,000 records each record is of size 256 byte. The disk consists of 512 byte per sector, 63 sector per track and total surfaces in disk are 10. Then the number of cylinder are needed to store the file is ____(integral value)?
solution:
Solution: step-by-step calculation to find the number of cylinders.

  • Total number of records = 70,000.

  • Each record size = 256 bytes; each sector size = 512 bytes.

  • Records per sector = 512 / 256 = 2 records per sector.

  • Sectors per track = 63; number of surfaces = 10.

  • Sectors per cylinder = sectors per track × number of surfaces = 63 × 10 = 630 sectors per cylinder.

  • Records per cylinder = sectors per cylinder × records per sector = 630 × 2 = 1260 records per cylinder.

  • Cylinders required = ceil(70,000 / 1260) = ceil(55.555...) = 56.

Answer: 56 cylinders

title: Storage Capacity of disk pack consisting of plates each having
subject: COA
text: Storage Capacity of a disk pack consisting of 4 plates each having 2655 tracks having 125 sectors per track, each sector having 512 bytes is approx.
solution:
Concept

The storage capacity of a magnetic disk pack is the product of all its geometric divisions. The governing identity is:

Capacity = (number of recording surfaces) × (tracks per surface) × (sectors per track) × (bytes per sector).

Multiplying these counts gives the total number of bytes, which is then converted to KB, MB or GB using the binary factor 1 KB = 1024 bytes (1 MB = 1024 KB, 1 GB = 1024 MB).

Application

Here the disk pack is specified directly by plates, so each plate contributes the stated 2655 tracks. Substituting the given values:

  1. Surfaces (plates) = 4, tracks per surface = 2655, so total tracks = 4 × 2655 = 10,620.

  2. Sectors = 10,620 × 125 = 1,327,500 sectors.

  3. Bytes = 1,327,500 × 512 = 679,680,000 bytes.

  4. Convert: 679,680,000 ÷ 1024 ≈ 663,750 KB ≈ 648 MB ≈ 0.63 GB (about two-thirds of a gigabyte).

Rounded to the nearest listed magnitude, this is approximately 1 GB.

Cross-check

Compare the result, ~0.65 GB, against each magnitude offered: it is a few hundred MB, i.e. on the order of 10⁸–10⁹ bytes. That sits squarely at the gigabyte scale — it is roughly a thousand times larger than a megabyte and roughly a thousand times smaller than a terabyte, and far above a few hundred KB. So the gigabyte-scale value is the only consistent approximation.

optionFeedback.html: The full product 4 × 2655 × 125 × 512 = 679,680,000 bytes is about 648 MB, just under two-thirds of a gigabyte, so a gigabyte-scale figure is the right order of magnitude for this disk pack.

This size results from leaving most of the geometry out of the product — for instance multiplying only one track's 125 sectors by 512 bytes and ignoring that there are 2655 tracks on each of the 4 surfaces. Every track and surface must be included before converting to a higher unit.

A terabyte assumes a unit far larger than the geometry supports. It typically comes from a conversion slip — for example carrying the byte count up by one unit too many (treating mega as tera), rather than from the multiplication of plates, tracks, sectors and bytes itself.

Around a megabyte's worth of kilobytes matches counting only a single track (or a fraction of the pack) rather than all 4 surfaces. The repeated factors for the 2655 tracks per surface and the 4 surfaces have been dropped from the product.
