title: Certain moving arm disk storage with one read/write head has
subject: COA
text: A certain moving arm disk storage with one read/write head has the following specifications: number of tracks per surface - 100, disk rotation speed 2400 RPM, track storage capacity of 32768 bits. If the average rotational latency is X msec and data transfer rate is Y bits/sec, what are the values of X and Y?
solution:
Disk rotation speed is given as 2400 RPM.

Means, 2400 rotations in 60 seconds.

Time for one rotation = 60 / 2400 seconds = 1/40 seconds = 25 ms

X = Average rotational latency = ½(Time for one rotation) = 25/2 = 12.5 ms

We know in one rotation one entire track can be read, that is in 25 ms we can read 32768 bits.

In one second we can read = 32768 / (25*10^-3) = 1.31 * 10^6 bits

Y = data transfer rate = 1.31 Mbits / sec

title: Certain moving arm disk storage with one read/write head has
subject: COA
text: A certain moving arm disk storage with one read/write head has the following specifications: number of tracks per surface - 400, disk rotation speed 6000 RPM, track storage capacity of 65,536 bits. If the average rotational latency is X msec and data transfer rate is Y Mbits/sec, what are the values of X and Y?
solution:
Step-by-step calculation:

  • Rotation speed: 6000 RPM = 6000/60 = 100 rotations per second. So one rotation takes 1/100 s = 0.01 s = 10 ms.

  • Average rotational latency = half a rotation = 10 ms / 2 = 5 ms

  • Data per rotation (one track) = 65,536 bits. Rotations per second = 100, so data transfer rate = 100 × 65,536 = 6,553,600 bits/sec

  • Expressed in common units: 6,553,600 bits/sec = 6.5536 Mbits/sec (decimal megabits). If using binary-based units, this equals 6,553,600 / (1024×1024) ≈ 6.25 Mibits/sec

Final answers: Average rotational latency = 5 ms. Data transfer rate = 6,553,600 bits/sec (≈ 6.5536 Mbits/sec or ≈ 6.25 Mibits/sec).

Interpreting that in common units: this equals 6.5536 Mbits/sec (decimal megabits) or 6.25 Mibits/sec (mebibits, using 1024×1024). title: Magnetic tape is consisting of some Kbits blocks. Inter block
subject: COA
text: A magnetic tape consists of blocks of size 32 Kbits each. The inter-block gap length is 0.2 inch, and the recording density is 4 KB/inch. If the tape length is 1000 feet, what is the total storage capacity of the tape?
solution:
Given data and key conversions:

  • Recording density = 4 KB per inch.

  • Tape length = 1000 feet = 1000 × 12 = 12,000 inches.

  • Each block capacity = 32 kilobits = 32/8 = 4 KB.

  • Block physical length = block capacity ÷ recording density = 4 KB ÷ (4 KB/inch) = 1 inch.

  • Inter-block gap = 0.2 inch, so space per block including gap = 1 + 0.2 = 1.2 inches.

Compute number of blocks:

  1. Number of blocks = total tape length in inches ÷ space per block = 12,000 ÷ 1.2 = 10,000 blocks.

Compute total storage (extra clarification because the provided choices are in MB):

  • Total data = number of blocks × block size = 10,000 × 4 KB = 40,000 KB.

  • Using decimal megabytes (1 MB = 1000 KB): 40,000 KB = 40 MB. If using binary megabytes (1 MiB = 1024 KB), this is about 39.06 MiB.

Final answers:

  • Number of blocks on the tape = 10,000.

  • Total storage capacity = 40,000 KB = 40 MB (decimal MB).

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The tape contains 10,000 blocks of 4 KB each, which equals 40,000 KB (40 MB). The value 20 MB would correspond to only 5,000 blocks (5,000 × 4 KB = 20,000 KB = 20 MB), so it underestimates the tape capacity.

Incorrect. The calculated number of blocks is 10,000, giving total storage 40,000 KB (40 MB). A value of 60 MB would correspond to 15,000 blocks (15,000 × 4 KB = 60,000 KB), which overestimates the tape capacity given the block length and gap.
Incorrect. The tape actually holds 10,000 blocks of 4 KB each = 40,000 KB (40 MB). The value 10 MB would correspond to only 2,500 blocks (2,500 × 4 KB = 10,000 KB), so it is too small.

Correct. Each block is 32 kilobits = 4 KB, block physical length = 4 KB ÷ (4 KB/inch) = 1 inch, plus a 0.2 inch gap gives 1.2 inches per block. 1000 ft = 12,000 inches, so number of blocks = 12,000 ÷ 1.2 = 10,000. Total data = 10,000 × 4 KB = 40,000 KB = 40 MB (using 1 MB = 1000 KB).

title: The time to access the first word of specific sector
subject: COA
text: The time to access the first word of a specific sector of a hard disk depends on rotational speed of the disk, the average seek time and the number of sectors per track. If we want to access the entire sector instead of one word (assume a sector holds about 100 words). How longer will it take to access a sector compared to one word?
solution:
Key idea: access time has three parts: seek time, rotational delay, and transfer time.

  • Seek time and rotational delay are fixed overheads paid once when accessing a sector.

  • Transfer time scales with the amount of data; reading 100 words makes the transfer component about 100 × the single-word transfer.

  • Total access time for a sector = seek time + rotational delay + (100 × transfer_time_per_word).

Example:

  • If seek = 8 ms, rotational = 4 ms, and transfer per word = 0.01 ms, then

  • One word: 8 + 4 + 0.01 = 12.01 ms

  • One sector (100 words): 8 + 4 + 1.0 = 13.0 ms

Conclusion: reading a full sector takes only a little longer than reading a single word (the extra is the transfer time). None of the numeric choices (10×, 20×, 100×) correctly describe the typical factor increase, so "none of the above" is the correct answer.

optionFeedback.html: The statement "10 times longer" is not correct. Reading a whole sector adds transfer time, but the total access time also includes seek time and rotational delay which are paid once. Because those fixed delays often dominate, the total time will not generally be 10 times larger just because a sector contains 100 words.

The statement "20 times longer" is not correct. Transfer time for more words scales with the number of words, but seek time and rotational latency are not multiplied. Therefore a 20× claim is unsupported; the increase depends on the relative sizes of transfer time and the fixed delays.

The statement "100 times longer" is misleading. While reading 100 words does make the transfer component about 100 times the single-word transfer, the overall access time includes seek time and rotational delay which are incurred once. Thus the total access time will not generally be 100 times longer.

The statement "none of the above" is correct. Access time = seek time + rotational delay + transfer time. Seek and rotational delay are paid once; reading 100 words multiplies the transfer component but does not multiply the fixed delays. As a result, reading a whole sector takes slightly longer than reading one word (by the added transfer time), but not 10×, 20×, or 100× in typical scenarios.

title: The total time to prepare disk drive mechanism for block
subject: COA
text: The total time to prepare a disk drive mechanism for a block of data to be read from it is
solution: To read data from a disk drive, the system must first prepare the mechanism by positioning the read head over the correct data block. This preparation involves two key steps: seek time and rotational latency. Seek time is the duration required for the disk arm to move the read head to the correct track where the data resides. Rotational latency is the time it takes for the desired sector to rotate under the read head once the correct track is reached. The total preparation time is the sum of these two components, making 'latency plus seek time' the correct answer. Transmission time is excluded because it refers to the actual data transfer duration, not the setup phase.

optionFeedback.html: Seek time is only the duration to position the head; it excludes the rotational delay required for the data to arrive.
Latency refers to the rotational delay; it does not account for the time needed to move the read head to the track.

Disk access preparation time consists of two main components: seek time to position the head over the correct track, and rotational latency to wait for the specific sector to spin under the head. These two times add up before data transfer begins.
Transmission time is the duration to transfer data after positioning, not part of the preparation phase.

title: Consider the following specifications of disk: An average seek time

text:

title: Which of the following is the major part of time
subject: COA
text: Which of the following is the major part of time taken when accessing data on the disk ?
solution:
Concept: The total time to access data on a disk is made up of several distinct delays that happen before the transfer itself: seek time (the read/write head physically moving to the correct track), rotational latency (waiting for the target sector to rotate under the head), and settle time (a brief pause for head vibration to damp out once it reaches the track). Because seek time involves mechanically repositioning the actuator arm — a comparatively slow, physical motion covering anywhere from one to hundreds of cylinders — it is typically the largest of these components, often several times longer than rotational latency and orders of magnitude longer than settle time.

Application: For this question, the head must first travel to the target track before any reading or writing can start, and that mechanical travel consistently takes longer (commonly several milliseconds) than the roughly half-a-revolution wait for rotational latency or the sub-millisecond settle time. This is exactly why disk-access-time analysis (and standard OS/COA references) identifies this head-positioning delay as the dominant, major part of total disk access time.

Cross-check — why the other listed timings are not the major part:

  • Settle time is only the microsecond-scale pause for head vibration to damp once positioning is done — a small fraction of the total, not the major part.

  • Rotational latency is bounded purely by the disk's spin speed (on average, half a revolution) — a real delay, but one that doesn't involve any mechanical repositioning, so it is generally smaller.

  • Waiting time (queueing time) is the delay a request spends waiting in a scheduling queue before the disk even starts servicing it — that is a contention/scheduling concept external to the disk's own physical access-time components, so it cannot itself be counted as part of the disk's access time.

optionFeedback.html: Settle time is the brief period for vibration damping after head movement. It contributes minimally to total disk access time compared to other components.

Rotational latency is the wait for the desired sector to rotate under the head, bounded by the disk's rotation speed — on average, about half a revolution. At typical spindle speeds this amounts to only a few milliseconds, a real but comparatively modest contributor to overall access time.

Seek time dominates disk access because the read/write head must physically move to the correct track. This mechanical movement takes significantly longer than rotational latency or data transfer time.

Waiting time refers to the time a request spends queued before disk access even begins. That is a scheduling/queueing concept, external to the disk's own physical access-time components, so it cannot itself be the major part of the disk's access time.

title: Consider the following statements: Comparing the time taken for single
subject: COA
text:
Consider the following statements:
S₁: Comparing the time T₁ taken for a single instruction on a pipelined CPU with time T₂ taken on a non-pipelined but identical CPU we can say that T₁ ≤ T₂.
S₂: The performance of pipelined processor suffers if the pipeline stages have different delays.
Which of the following option is correct?

options.html: None of S₁ or S₂ is correct

solution:
S₁ is false (not necessarily true).

  • Pipelining improves throughput, not necessarily the latency of a single instruction. The latency of one instruction in a pipelined CPU equals the sum of stage delays plus any pipeline-register overhead. A non-pipelined (monolithic) implementation does the whole work in one cycle whose delay might equal the same sum without the register overhead. Thus a pipelined instruction can have equal or larger latency, not necessarily smaller. So the claim T1≤T2T_1 \le T_2T1​≤T2​ is not guaranteed.

S₂ is true.

  • If pipeline stages have different delays, the clock period must accommodate the slowest stage; faster stages idle waiting for the clock. This increases the cycle time and reduces pipeline throughput (performance), so performance suffers.

Final answer: S₁ — False, S₂ — True.

title: The performance of pipelined processor suffers if
subject: COA
text: The performance of a pipelined processor suffers if

options.html: consecutive instructions are dependent on each other

solution: Pipelined processor performance suffers due to pipeline imbalance, where the clock cycle matches the slowest stage causing idle time. Data hazards introduce stalls or bubbles when instructions depend on unavailable results. Structural hazards cause delays due to resource contention. Since all these scenarios negatively impact throughput and efficiency, the correct choice is All of the above.

optionFeedback.html: Uneven stage delays force the clock cycle to match the slowest stage, limiting throughput.
Instruction dependencies create data hazards that require stalls or bubbles in the pipeline.
Structural hazards occur when pipeline stages compete for shared hardware resources, causing stalls.
Multiple factors including resource contention and data dependencies contribute to pipeline performance degradation.

title: Consider the program which was made to run on two
subject: COA
text: Consider the program which was made to run on two different machines the machine 2 results 30% speeder however the CPI is increased by 25%. If the clock frequency of the machine 1 is 2 MHZ what is the clock frequency of machine 2?
solution:
• Machine 2 is 30% faster than Machine 1 (i.e., performance2 = 1.3 × performance1).

  • CPI on Machine 2 is 25% higher than Machine 1: CPI2 = 1.25 × CPI1.

  • Clock frequency of Machine 1: f1 = 2 MHz.

  • Find clock frequency f2 of Machine 2.

Definitions and relations

  • Execution time T = IC × CPI / f (IC = instruction count; same for both machines).

  • Performance ∝ 1 / T.

  • Given performance2 = 1.3 × performance1 ⇒ T2 = T1 / 1.3.

Compute ratio T2/T1 using the execution-time formula: T2/T1 = (IC·CPI2 / f2) / (IC·CPI1 / f1) = (CPI2 / CPI1) · (f1 / f2)

Set equal to 1/1.3: (CPI2 / CPI1) · (f1 / f2) = 1 / 1.3

Rearrange to solve for f2: f2 / f1 = 1.3 × (CPI2 / CPI1)

Substitute CPI2 / CPI1 = 1.25: f2 / f1 = 1.3 × 1.25 = 1.625

Therefore: f2 = 1.625 × f1 = 1.625 × 2 MHz = 3.25 MHz

Quick numeric check

Assume IC = 1 and CPI1 = 1 for simplicity:

  • T1 = 1 / 2 = 0.5 (time units)

  • CPI2 = 1.25 → T2 = 1.25 / 3.25 ≈ 0.384615

  • T1 / T2 ≈ 0.5 / 0.384615 = 1.3 ⇒ performance2 is 30% higher ✔

Answer: f2 = 3.25 MHz.

title: What is the main advantage of instruction pipelining
subject: COA
text: What is the main advantage of instruction pipelining?
solution:
Instruction pipelining splits instruction execution into stages (fetch, decode, execute, memory access, write-back) and overlaps these stages across successive instructions, so a new instruction enters the pipeline before the previous one has fully finished. Because several instructions are in flight simultaneously, the average time to complete each instruction, and hence overall throughput, improves, even though a single instruction's total latency through all stages is unchanged.

Applying this here: the direct effect of that stage-overlap is a lower average completion time per instruction, which is exactly what makes 'Reduced instruction execution time' the main advantage being asked about.

Checking each other option against this by value:

  • Increased memory access speed, a cache/RAM property, not something pipelining's stage-overlap changes.

  • Improved data transfer rate, a bus/interconnect bandwidth property, again unrelated to overlapping instruction stages.

  • All of these, fails because the two properties above are unaffected by pipelining, so grouping them with execution time overstates pipelining's effect.

optionFeedback.html: Memory access speed is governed by the cache/RAM hierarchy, a separate hardware concern from how instruction stages overlap in the pipeline. Pipelining changes how quickly instructions move through execution, not how fast memory itself responds.

Overlapping the fetch-decode-execute-memory-write-back stages across successive instructions lets a new instruction start before the previous one finishes, directly cutting the average time to complete each instruction and raising overall throughput.
Data transfer rate is a bus/interconnect bandwidth property, how much data moves per unit time between components, which pipelining's stage-overlap does not touch.

This only holds if pipelining improved every property listed. Memory access speed and data transfer rate are untouched by stage-overlap, so bundling them together overstates what pipelining actually changes.

title: The right sequence of suboperations that are performed in arithmetic
subject: COA
text:
The right sequence of suboperations that are performed in arithmetic pipeline is –
A. Align the mantissas
B. Add or subtract the mantissas
C. Normalize the result
D. Compare the exponents
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution:
Correct sequence: Compare the exponents → Align the mantissas → Add or subtract the mantissas → Normalize the result.

  1. Step 1 — Compare the exponents: Determine which operand has the larger exponent so you know which mantissa (if any) must be shifted.

  2. Step 2 — Align the mantissas: Shift the mantissa of the operand with the smaller exponent to match the larger exponent (align the binary points).

  3. Step 3 — Add or subtract the mantissas: Perform the arithmetic on the aligned mantissas.

  4. Step 4 — Normalize the result: If the result's mantissa is out of range, shift it and adjust the exponent accordingly; then apply rounding if required.

Why other orders fail:

  • Trying to add or subtract before aligning produces incorrect results because the binary points do not match.

  • Normalizing before the arithmetic makes no sense because normalization depends on the arithmetic result.

  • Alignment requires knowing which exponent is larger, so exponent comparison must come first.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. First compare the exponents to determine which operand has the larger exponent. Shift the mantissa of the operand with the smaller exponent to align the binary points (align the mantissas). Perform the arithmetic (add or subtract) on the aligned mantissas. Finally normalize the result by shifting the mantissa and adjusting the exponent as needed.

Incorrect. This sequence attempts to add or subtract the mantissas before aligning them. You must compare exponents and then align the mantissas (shift the smaller one) before performing addition or subtraction; otherwise the arithmetic will be incorrect.

Incorrect. This sequence starts with alignment before comparing exponents, but you must first compare exponents to know which mantissa to shift. It also normalizes before performing the arithmetic; normalization should occur after the add/subtract step.
Incorrect. You cannot align mantissas correctly without first comparing exponents to see which operand needs shifting. Also, normalization should occur after addition/subtraction, not before.

title: Consider stage pipeline system. Assume that there is no cycle
subject: COA
text: Consider a 5-stage pipeline system. Assume that there is no cycle-time overhead of pipelining. An application is executing on this pipeline system. What is the speedup achieved with respect to non-pipelined execution if 42% of the instructions incur 2 pipeline stall cycles? ______ (up to 2 decimal places)
solution:
Concept: In an ideal pipeline one instruction completes every clock cycle, so the pipelined machine needs 1 cycle per instruction and every stall cycle adds directly on top of it: CPIpipelined = 1 + (average stall cycles per instruction). A non-pipelined machine has no overlap at all — it must finish all k stage-cycles of one instruction before starting the next — so CPInon-pipelined = k.

When pipelining adds no cycle-time overhead, both machines run at the same clock period, so the cycle counts alone decide the ratio: Speedup = k / (1 + average stall cycles per instruction).

Application: substituting the data given in this question.

  1. Pipeline depth k = 5, so the non-pipelined machine spends 5 cycles per instruction.

  2. Average stall cycles per instruction = (fraction of instructions that stall) × (penalty per stall) = 0.42 × 2 = 0.84.

  3. CPIpipelined = 1 + 0.84 = 1.84 cycles per instruction.

  4. Speedup = 5 / 1.84 = 2.7173913…

Cross-check: multiplying back, 1.84 × 2.71739 ≈ 5.00, which recovers the non-pipelined cycle count, so the ratio is consistent. The value also lies inside the expected bounds — with no stalls at all the speedup would be the full depth 5, and 0.84 stall cycles per instruction pull it down to roughly 2.72.

Answer: Speedup = 5 / 1.84 = 2.7173913… . Expressed to two decimal places this is 2.71 if the remaining digits are truncated and 2.72 if they are rounded, so both 2.71 and 2.72 are accepted.

text: A five-stage pipeline has stage delays of 50, 60, 80, 75, 80 and 70 nanoseconds. Answer: 45360 ns

title: The instruction pipeline of processor has the following stages: IF
subject: COA
text: The instruction pipeline of a processor has the following stages: IF (instruction fetch), ID (instruction decode), OF (operand fetch), PO (perform operation), and WB (write back). The IF, ID, OF and WB stages take 1 clock cycle each for every instruction. Consider a sequence of 50 instructions. Assume that there are no data hazards and no control hazards. The number of clock cycles required for completion of execution of the sequence of instructions is ?
solution:
Key idea: The pipeline has 5 stages (IF, ID, OF, PO, WB). If every stage took 1 cycle, the total cycles for 50 instructions would be number of instructions + number of stages - 1 = 50 + 5 - 1 = 54.

Variable PO stage: each instruction i spends k_i cycles in the PO stage. Each instruction that needs more than 1 cycle in PO causes (k_i - 1) extra stall cycles.

  • Total PO cycles = 20×3 + 18×2 + 12×1 = 60 + 36 + 12 = 108.

  • Total extra stall cycles = (sum of PO cycles) - (number of instructions) = 108 - 50 = 58.

  • Total cycles = base pipeline cycles (54) + total stalls (58) = 112 cycles.

Answer: 112 cycles.

title: Consider the two processors and MIPS Million instruction per second)
subject: COA
text: Consider the two processors P1 and P2. MIPS ( Million instruction per second) of P1 is 100 and P2 is 200. Which of the following options are correct?
solution:
Short answer: Using only MIPS you cannot determine which processor is better.

  • Key formula for performance: Execution time = (Instruction count × CPI) / Clock rate

  • Relation to MIPS: MIPS = (Instruction count / Execution time) / 10^6, which can also be expressed as Clock rate / (CPI × 10^6) for a given instruction mix. MIPS depends on CPI and the instruction mix, so it can be misleading across different architectures or compilers.

  • Illustrative example: Suppose P1 reports 100 MIPS and P2 reports 200 MIPS. If a program requires 50 million instructions on P1, its execution time on P1 = 50,000,000 / (100,000,000 instructions/sec) = 0.5 s. If the same task requires 200 million instructions on P2, its execution time on P2 = 200,000,000 / (200,000,000 instructions/sec) = 1.0 s. Here P1 is faster despite lower MIPS, showing why MIPS alone is inadequate.

  • Recommendation: Compare processors using execution time for representative workloads or standardized benchmarks (for example SPEC). When needed, use Instruction count, CPI, and clock rate together to compute and compare real performance.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. You cannot conclude that P1 is a better processor based only on the given MIPS values. MIPS measures instruction throughput but does not account for instruction complexity, cycles per instruction (CPI), or how many instructions a program needs. To compare processors, use actual program execution time or other comprehensive benchmarks.

Not necessarily correct. Although P2 has a higher MIPS value, higher MIPS does not guarantee better real-world performance. MIPS can be misleading because it ignores instruction mix and CPI. The correct way to compare is to compute execution time for the same task or use standard benchmarks.

Incorrect. The two processors do not necessarily have the same capability simply because we have two MIPS numbers. Capability and performance depend on instruction set, CPI, clock rate, and how many instructions are required for a given task, not just the MIPS values.

Correct. MIPS alone is not sufficient to decide which processor is better. To compare processors reliably, compute execution time for a real workload (Execution time = Instruction count * CPI / Clock rate) or use standardized benchmarks. MIPS can be misleading because a processor with lower MIPS might require fewer instructions to complete the same task and thus be faster.

subject: COA
text: A non-pipeline processor has a clock rate 4 MHz and an average CPI of 5. An upgrade to the processor introduces 5 stage pipeline. However, due to internal delay the clock rate of the new processor has to be reduced to 3 MHz. What is the speed-up of pipeline over non-pipeline?
solution:
Step-by-step calculation:

  1. Non-pipeline processor:

    Cycle time = 1 / clock rate = 1 / 4 MHz = 0.25 μs. Execution time per instruction = average CPI × cycle time = 5 × 0.25 μs = 1.25 μs.

  2. Pipelined processor (5-stage):

    New cycle time = 1 / 3 MHz = 0.333... μs. With an ideal pipeline throughput of one instruction per cycle, execution time per instruction ≈ 1 × 0.333... μs = 0.333... μs.

  3. Speed-up calculation:

    Speed-up = execution time (non-pipeline) / execution time (pipeline) = 1.25 μs / 0.333... μs = 3.75.

    If the pipeline cycle time is approximated as 0.33 μs, the quoted approximate value becomes about 3.78; the exact ratio using repeating decimal 0.333... is 3.75.

Final answer: The speed-up of the pipelined processor over the non-pipelined one is 3.75 (which lies within the provided range 3.7–3.78).

title: How many cycles are required for MHz processor to execute
subject: COA
text: How many cycles are required for a 100 MHz processor to execute a program which requires 10 seconds of CPU time?
solution:
Solution:

Method 1 (direct multiplication):

  • Processor frequency = 100 MHz = 100 × 10^6 cycles per second.

  • Time = 10 seconds.

  • Total cycles = frequency × time = 100 × 10^6 × 10 = 1 × 10^9 cycles.

Method 2 (using cycle time):

  • Cycle time = 1 / (100 × 10^6) = 1 × 10^-8 s = 10 ns.

  • Total time = 10 s = 10 × 10^9 ns.

  • Total cycles = total time / cycle time = (10 × 10^9 ns) / 10 ns = 1 × 10^9 cycles.

Answer: 1 × 10^9 cycles.

title: If microcomputer operates at MHz with an 8-bit bus and
subject: COA
text: If a microcomputer operates at 5 MHz with an 8-bit bus and a newer version operates at 20 MHz with a 32-bit bus, the maximum speed-up possible approximately will be
solution:
Concept

When a system is upgraded along two independent performance dimensions, the maximum theoretical speed-up is the PRODUCT of the individual improvement factors, not their sum. Each factor is an independent multiplier on throughput, so the gains compound.

For a bus-based microcomputer, data throughput is proportional to (clock frequency) × (bus width): the clock frequency sets how many bus cycles occur per second, and the bus width sets how many bits move per cycle. Improving either one multiplies throughput; improving both multiplies the two multipliers together.

Application

  1. Clock-frequency factor = new clock ÷ old clock = 20 MHz ÷ 5 MHz = 4.

  2. Bus-width factor = new width ÷ old width = 32-bit ÷ 8-bit = 4.

  3. Maximum speed-up = (clock factor) × (bus factor) = 4 × 4 = 16.

Cross-check / contrast

  • Using only the clock factor gives 4 — this ignores the wider bus, so it understates the gain.

  • Adding the factors gives 4 + 4 = 8 — independent throughput multipliers compound, they are never added.

  • A value of 2 reflects neither factor fully and corresponds to no consistent calculation from the given figures.

  • Only the product 4 × 4 = 16 captures both independent improvements together, so it is the maximum theoretical speed-up.

optionFeedback.html: A value of 2 is far too small to match an upgrade of this scale. It does not arise from the figures in the question under any reasonable reading of how performance changes here, so it can be set aside as an underestimate.

A value of 4 stops after accounting for just one of the changes described in the question and treats the rest of the upgrade as if it had no effect. Because the question asks for the maximum overall speed-up, settling on a single change leaves part of the improvement unused.

A value of 8 comes from a plausible-looking but incorrect way of combining the two changes. The individual changes are read correctly, yet they are brought together using the wrong arithmetic step, which is why the result lands short of the true maximum.

A value of 16 is the maximum theoretical speed-up: the clock frequency rises by a factor of 4 (20 versus 5) and the bus width rises by a factor of 4 (32 versus 8), and because these are independent throughput multipliers they compound to 4 × 4 = 16.

title: Consider an instruction pipeline with four stages and each with
subject: COA
text:
Consider an instruction pipeline with four stages (S1, S2, S3 and S4), each with a combinational circuit only. The pipeline registers are required between each stage and at the end of the last stage. Delays for the stages and for the pipeline registers are as given in the following figure:

What is the approximate speed up of the pipeline in steady state under ideal conditions when compared to the corresponding non-pipeline implementation?
solution:
Concept

In a pipeline whose stages take unequal amounts of time, the pipeline's clock cycle time is fixed by the slowest stage plus the delay of the pipeline register (latch) that follows it -- every stage must wait for the longest stage to finish and for the register to latch its output before the next cycle can start. Once the pipeline is full (steady state), one instruction completes every clock cycle, so the achievable speedup over a non-pipelined implementation is the ratio of the total non-pipelined execution time to this single pipeline clock cycle time.

Application

  1. Non-pipelined execution time per instruction is the sum of all four stage delays: 5 + 6 + 11 + 8 = 30 ns.

  2. The slowest stage is S3, with a delay of 11 ns.

  3. The pipeline clock cycle equals the slowest stage delay plus the pipeline-register delay: 11 + 1 = 12 ns.

  4. Steady-state speedup equals the non-pipelined time divided by the pipeline clock cycle: 30 / 12 = 2.5.

Cross-check

If all four combinational stages had the same delay d, the speedup with a 1 ns register overhead would be 4d / (d + 1), approaching the stage-count ceiling of 4 only when the register overhead is negligible relative to d. Here the unequal stage delays make the 11 ns stage the bottleneck, and substituting the actual 12 ns clock interval gives 30 / 12 = 2.5.

For a candidate speedup of 2.5, a 30 ns non-pipelined time corresponds to a completion interval of 30 / 2.5 = 12 ns.
For a candidate speedup of 1.1, a 30 ns non-pipelined time corresponds to a completion interval of approximately 30 / 1.1 = 27.3 ns.
For a candidate speedup of 3.0, a 30 ns non-pipelined time corresponds to a completion interval of 30 / 3.0 = 10 ns.

title: Which of the following statements with respect to K-segment pipelining
subject: COA
text:
Which of the following statements with respect to K-segment pipelining are true?

(A)  Maximum speedup that a pipeline can provide is 𝑘 theoretically

(B)  It is impossible to achieve maximum speed up 𝑘 in 𝑘-segment pipeline

(C)  All segments in pipeline take same time in computation

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution:
Final answer: The correct true statements are the one that says the theoretical maximum speedup of a k-segment pipeline is k and the one that says it is impossible (in practical terms) to achieve that maximum. The claim that all segments take the same time is not generally true.

Explanation:

  • Theoretical upper bound on speedup: For a k-segment pipeline, the ideal (theoretical) maximum speedup is k. This assumes perfectly balanced stages, no pipeline register overhead, no hazards, and a steady stream of independent tasks.

  • Practical achievability: In practice, achieving the ideal k-fold speedup is effectively impossible because of register and latch overhead, imbalanced stage latencies, pipeline hazards (data, control, structural), and the cycles needed to fill and drain the pipeline. So the statement that reaching the theoretical maximum is impossible is intended in a practical sense and is correct as a real-world observation.

  • Equal-stage-time claim: It is not generally true that all segments take the same time. Equal stage durations are an ideal design goal to maximize utilization, but real pipelines often have unequal stage latencies; the slowest stage determines the pipeline clock period and thus limits speedup.

  • Conclusion: The theoretical maximum is k (true), the practical impossibility of reaching that maximum is a valid real-world statement (true in practice), and the claim that all segments take equal time is false in general. Therefore the correct selection includes the first two statements only.

optionFeedback.html: Correct selection. The statement that the theoretical maximum speedup of a k-segment pipeline is k is true: in an ideal, perfectly balanced pipeline with no overhead, the best possible speedup is k. The statement that it is impossible to achieve that maximum refers to practical reality: pipeline register overhead, stage imbalances, hazards, and the time to fill and drain the pipeline make reaching the ideal k-fold speedup effectively impossible in real implementations. The statement that all segments take the same time is not generally true, so the combination containing the first two statements only is correct.

Incorrect. The claim that all pipeline segments take the same time is not generally true; segment durations vary in real designs and the slowest stage limits throughput. While it's reasonable to say achieving the ideal k speedup is practically unattainable, pairing that with the equal-stage-time claim makes this combination wrong.

Incorrect. The theoretical maximum speedup being k is correct, but the claim that all segments take the same time is not generally true. Also, practical limitations (register overhead, hazards, fill/drain) mean the ideal k speedup is seldom achieved; omitting that practical caveat makes this choice incomplete.

Incorrect. The statement that all segments take the same time is not generally true in real pipelines. Including that statement makes the triple selection incorrect even though the theoretical maximum speedup is k and practical limitations make achieving it unlikely.

title: Consider an instruction pipeline as shown below: program having instructions
subject: COA
text:
Consider an instruction pipeline as shown below:


A program having 80 instructions is executed in the pipelined processor. Instruction I6 is the unconditional jump instruction and branch address is known after EX stage. The time needed to complete the execution of the program if the branch target address is 78th instruction is ________________ns
solution:
Key idea: the pipeline has four stages (IF, ID, EX, MO) and buffer delays between stages. The clock period must accommodate the longest stage plus its following buffer delay.

  • Compute clock period: the EX stage is 6 ns and the buffer after EX is 3 ns, so clock period = 6 + 3 = 9 ns.

Which instructions actually execute: the program executes instructions 1 through 6, then instruction 6 is an unconditional jump to instruction 78, so the executed instructions are 1–6 and 78–80, a total of 9 instructions.

Cycle count and branch penalty:

  • Base pipeline cycles without hazards = number of executed instructions + (pipeline depth − 1) = 9 + 3 = 12.

  • Because the branch (instruction 6) is resolved in the EX stage, two following instructions (the ones fetched in the two cycles between the branch IF and branch EX) are speculatively fetched and must be flushed, adding a penalty of 2 cycles.

  • Total cycles = base cycles + branch flush penalty = 12 + 2 = 14 cycles.

Total time = total cycles × clock period = 14 × 9 ns = 126 ns.

title: Assume an instruction mix of conditional branches, unconditional branches, all
subject: COA
text:
Assume an instruction mix of 20% conditional branches, 5% unconditional branches, 75% all others. 65% of the conditional branches are taken. We have a 5-stage pipeline where branch target locations are computed in the 2nd stage and branch conditions in the 4th stage. Assume no other sources of pipeline stalls.

We want to decide whether to implement "predict taken" or "predict not taken" for branch prediction for this machine. For "predict not taken", even unconditional branches are assumed not taken. Which of the following is correct?

options.html: "predict taken" is better for this machine.
"predict not taken" is better for this machine.
For "predict taken" branch predictions, CPI is the 1.54
For "predict not taken" branch predictions, CPI is the 1.54

solution:
We compare the two static strategies by computing the average branch penalty per instruction and the resulting CPI (base CPI = 1).

Predict taken:

  • Taken conditional branches (20% * 65%): resolved at stage 2 → 1-cycle penalty when predicted taken: 0.2 * 0.65 * 1 = 0.13

  • Not-taken conditional branches (20% * 35%): mispredicted until the condition is resolved at stage 4 → 3-cycle penalty: 0.2 * 0.35 * 3 = 0.21

  • Unconditional branches (5%): treated as taken → 1-cycle penalty: 0.05 * 1 = 0.05

Total branch penalty = 0.13 + 0.21 + 0.05 = 0.39, so CPI = 1 + 0.39 = 1.39.

Predict not taken:

  • Taken conditional branches (20% * 65%): mispredicted until stage 4 → 3-cycle penalty: 0.2 * 0.65 * 3 = 0.39

  • Not-taken conditional branches (20% * 35%): correctly predicted → 0-cycle penalty: 0.2 * 0.35 * 0 = 0

  • Unconditional branches (5%): mispredicted (predicted not taken) → 3-cycle penalty: 0.05 * 3 = 0.15

Total branch penalty = 0.39 + 0 + 0.15 = 0.54, so CPI = 1 + 0.54 = 1.54.

Conclusion: predicting taken is better because it gives a lower CPI (1.39) than predicting not taken (1.54).

optionFeedback.html: Correct. Using the given frequencies and penalties, predicting taken yields a branch penalty of 0.39 cycles and a CPI of 1.39 (1 + 0.39), which is lower than the CPI for predicting not taken. Therefore predicting taken is the better choice.

Incorrect. Predicting not taken gives a higher branch penalty of 0.54 cycles and a CPI of 1.54 (1 + 0.54). This happens because taken conditional branches and all unconditional branches incur the longer 3-cycle penalty when predicted not taken, so predicting not taken is worse here.
Incorrect. The CPI for the predict-taken strategy is 1.39, not 1.54. Calculation: branch penalty = 0.2*0.65*1 + 0.2*0.35*3 + 0.05*1 = 0.39, so CPI = 1 + 0.39 = 1.39.
Correct. For predicting not taken, branch penalty = 0.2*0.65*3 + 0.2*0.35*0 + 0.05*3 = 0.54 cycles, so CPI = 1 + 0.54 = 1.54. This is higher than the CPI for predicting taken (1.39).

subject: COA

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q90
subject: COA
text: In a 5-stage pipeline, branch is resolved in EX stage. If branch frequency = 15% and misprediction penalty = 2 cycles, what is pipeline CPI?
solution:
Concept: In a pipelined processor achieving an ideal one-cycle-per-instruction throughput, the baseline CPI is 1. Any instruction that forces the pipeline to stall raises the effective CPI above this baseline. A branch instruction whose outcome is not known until a later pipeline stage forces the pipeline to stall for a fixed number of cycles on every occurrence; this fixed per-branch stall cost is the branch (misprediction) penalty. Since the item supplies only a single branch frequency and a single fixed penalty value, with no separate misprediction-rate figure, the standard convention for this class of numerical is to apply that penalty uniformly to every branch instruction encountered. Averaged over all instructions, the overall CPI is: CPI = Ideal CPI + (Branch Frequency x Branch Penalty).

Application:

  1. Identify the given quantities: ideal CPI = 1 (one instruction completes per cycle in a hazard-free pipeline); branch frequency = 15% = 0.15 (fraction of instructions that are branches); branch penalty = 2 cycles (stall cycles incurred per branch, since the outcome is known only in the EX stage).

  2. Compute the average stall contributed by branch instructions: Stall per instruction = Branch Frequency x Branch Penalty = 0.15 x 2 = 0.30 cycles.

  3. Add this stall contribution to the ideal CPI: CPI = 1 + 0.30 = 1.30.

Cross-check with a per-100-instruction count: out of 100 instructions, 15 are branches; each branch adds 2 stall cycles, giving 15 x 2 = 30 extra cycles; total cycles = 100 (base) + 30 (stalls) = 130 cycles; CPI = total cycles / total instructions = 130 / 100 = 1.3, which matches the formula result.

Hence, the pipeline CPI is 1.3.

title: Which of the following is/are cause hazard in pipelined CPU
subject: COA
text: Which of the following is/are cause hazard in pipelined CPU ?

options.html: 2 consecutive instruction and both need to read memory at same time.
2 consecutive instructions and one instruction uses the result of previous instruction.

solution:
Explanation: The following situations each cause a hazard in a pipelined CPU:

  • Structural hazard — Two consecutive instructions both trying to read memory at the same time compete for the same hardware resource (for example, a single memory port), causing a stall or conflict. Mitigations include adding memory ports or caches, or stalling.

  • Control hazard — An instruction that contains a jump or branch creates uncertainty about the next instruction address until the branch is resolved. Common solutions include branch prediction, delayed branches, and pipeline flushing or stalling.

  • Data hazard — When one instruction uses the result produced by the immediately preceding instruction, a read-after-write dependency arises. Mitigations include forwarding/bypassing, instruction scheduling, or inserting stalls.

Conclusion: The three described situations (simultaneous memory reads, a jump/branch instruction, and an instruction using a previous result) are all causes of pipeline hazards. Therefore, the statement that none of these is a hazard is incorrect.

optionFeedback.html: Two consecutive instructions that both need to read memory at the same time cause a structural hazard because they compete for the same memory port or other hardware resource. Possible resolutions include adding separate instruction/data memory ports or caches, providing additional memory ports, or stalling one instruction until the resource is free.

An instruction that contains a jump or branch creates a control hazard because the next instruction to fetch depends on the branch outcome. Common mitigations include branch prediction, delayed branching, or flushing/stalling the pipeline until the branch target is known.

Two consecutive instructions where one uses the result of the previous instruction create a data hazard (specifically a read-after-write dependency). This can be handled with techniques such as forwarding/bypassing, instruction reordering, or inserting pipeline stalls.

'none of these' is incorrect because the first three statements describe valid pipeline hazards: simultaneous memory reads (structural), a jump/branch instruction (control), and using a prior result (data).

subject: COA
text:
Consider the following set of instructions executed for a program to be accomplished.

How many anti data dependencies and true data dependencies are present in the above instructions?
solution:
Concept

A pipeline's true (data) dependency — RAW, Read-After-Write — exists whenever an instruction reads a register whose value was produced by the nearest earlier instruction that wrote it; every such governed read counts as one dependency. An anti-dependency — WAR, Write-After-Read — exists whenever a later instruction writes a register that an earlier instruction had already read, because letting that write happen too soon would return the earlier instruction the wrong value. Both types are counted per read-write pair across the full instruction sequence, not merely between instructions that sit next to each other.

Application

First list every register this six-instruction sequence reads from and writes to:

Instruction

Reads

Writes

I1: STORE M[100], R1

R1

—

I2: MOV R2, M[700]

—

R2

I3: DIV R1, R2, R1

R2, R1

R1

I4: ADD R2, R1, R2

R1, R2

R2

I5: STORE M[500], R2

R2

—

I6: STORE M[200], R1

R1

—

Anti-dependencies (WAR) — an earlier instruction reads a register that a later instruction then writes:

  1. R1: I1 reads R1, and I3 later writes R1 — one anti-dependency.

  2. R2: I3 reads R2, and I4 later writes R2 — one anti-dependency.

  3. No other earlier-read-then-later-write pair exists for R1 or R2 across the sequence, so the anti-dependency count is 2.

True dependencies (RAW) — an instruction reads a register whose most recent value came from an earlier write:

  1. R1 is written only once, by I3. Every later read of R1 traces back to that same write, since nothing else writes R1 afterward: I4 reads R1 after I3, and I6 reads R1 after I3 — 2 true dependencies from R1.

  2. R2 is written twice — first by I2, then later by I4. I3 reads R2 before I4's write, so I3's value comes from I2. I4 also reads R2 as a source operand before its own write takes effect, so that read also comes from I2. After I4 writes R2, I5 reads R2, so I5's value comes from I4 — 3 true dependencies from R2 (two tracing to I2, one to I4).

  3. Total true dependencies = 2 (from R1) + 3 (from R2) = 5.

Cross-check

Confirm by tracing each register's own access timeline in program order:

Register

Access sequence (in program order)

R1

I1 reads → I3 reads and writes → I4 reads → I6 reads

R2

I2 writes → I3 reads → I4 reads and writes → I5 reads

Reading this timeline left to right and drawing an edge from every write to every read that follows it before the next write reproduces the same 5 true dependencies found above; drawing an edge from every read to the next write that follows it reproduces the same 2 anti-dependencies. A narrower check that only compares directly consecutive instructions (I1-I2, I2-I3, I3-I4, I4-I5, I5-I6) misses non-adjacent pairs — such as I1's read of R1 reaching all the way to I3's write, or I2's write of R2 still governing I4's read — and undercounts both totals.

So this instruction sequence contains 2 anti-dependencies (WAR) and 5 true dependencies (RAW).

optionFeedback.html: One checkpoint for verifying this pairing: I5 reads R2 using the value most recently written to R2, which is the value I4 writes, since no instruction between I4 and I5 writes to R2.
One checkpoint for verifying this pairing: I6 reads R1 using the value most recently written to R1, which is the value I3 writes, since no instruction between I3 and I6 writes to R1.

One checkpoint for verifying this pairing: I4 reads R2 as one of its source operands, before I4's own write to R2 takes effect, using the value most recently written to R2 at that point, which is the value I2 writes, since no instruction between I2 and I4 writes to R2.
One checkpoint for verifying this pairing: I1 reads R1 before any instruction in this sequence has written to R1, and R1 is later written by I3.

title: The following assembly code is to be executed in 3-stage
subject: COA
text:
The following assembly code is to be executed in a 3-stage pipelined processor with hazard detection and resolution in each stage. The stage are IF, OF (one or more as required) and execution (including write-back operation). What are the number of possible RAW, WAW and WAR hazards in the execution of the code.
Instruction Meaning
I₁: Inc R₀ R₀ ← (R₀) + 1
I₂: Mul ACC, R₀ ACC ← (ACC) × (R₀)
I₃: Store R₁, ACC R₁ ← (ACC)
I₄: Add ACC, R₀ ACC ← (ACC) + (R₀)
I₅: Store M, ACC M ← (ACC)
solution:
Final answer: RAW = 5, WAW = 1, WAR = 2

Definitions:

  • RAW (read after write): a later instruction reads a location that an earlier instruction writes.

  • WAW (write after write): two instructions write the same location; the order of writes matters.

  • WAR (write after read): an earlier instruction reads a location that a later instruction writes.

Identify hazards by location touched (R0, ACC, R1, M) and by instruction order.

RAW hazards (5 pairs):

  • I1 → I2 (I1 writes R0; I2 reads R0)

  • I1 → I4 (I1 writes R0; I4 reads R0)

  • I2 → I3 (I2 writes ACC; I3 reads ACC)

  • I2 → I4 (I2 writes ACC; I4 reads ACC)

  • I2 → I5 (I2 writes ACC; I5 reads ACC)

WAW hazards (1 pair):

  • I2 → I4 (both write ACC)

WAR hazards (2 pairs):

  • I3 → I4 (I3 reads ACC; I4 later writes ACC)

  • I2 → I4 (I2 reads ACC as source and I4 later writes ACC)

Notes: The same instruction pair can appear in more than one hazard category when one instruction both reads and writes the same location (for example, the pair I2 → I4 is both a RAW and a WAW/WAR interaction depending on which access is considered). The final tallies under the pipeline timing given are RAW = 5, WAW = 1, WAR = 2.

optionFeedback.html: The answer '6, 1, 2' is not correct. The WAW and WAR counts (1 and 2) match the correct solution, but the RAW count is 5, not 6. The correct RAW pairs are: I1 → I2, I1 → I4, I2 → I3, I2 → I4, and I2 → I5. One might be tempted to add I4 → I5, but under the pipeline timing assumed here that pair does not produce an additional RAW hazard.

The answer '5, 3, 3' has the RAW count correct (5) but the WAW and WAR counts are too large. There is only one WAW hazard: I2 → I4 (both write ACC). The correct WAR hazards are two pairs: I3 → I4 and I2 → I4. So the correct tuple is 5, 1, 2.

The answer '5, 3, 2' gets the RAW and WAR counts right (5 and 2) but the WAW count is incorrect. Only one WAW occurs: I2 → I4 (both instructions write ACC). Reduce the WAW count from 3 to 1 to match the correct solution 5, 1, 2.

The answer '5, 1, 2' is correct. RAW hazards (5): I1 → I2, I1 → I4, I2 → I3, I2 → I4, I2 → I5. WAW hazards (1): I2 → I4 (both write ACC). WAR hazards (2): I3 → I4 and I2 → I4 (earlier reads conflicted with later writes). The counts and listed pairs match the pipeline hazard analysis for the given 3-stage pipeline.

Let A be the number of true (RAW) dependencies, B the number of anti (WAR) dependencies, and C the number of output (WAW) dependencies. Find A + B + C.
solution:
CONCEPT

A dependency is identified from the read and write order of the same register. RAW means a later instruction reads a value written earlier; WAR means a later instruction writes a register read earlier; WAW means two instructions write the same register.

The scope here is register dependencies within one loop iteration. Memory-location dependencies and loop-carried dependencies are therefore outside the count.

  1. RAW dependencies: I1 → I2 through R1; I2 → I3 through R1; and I5 → I6 through R4. Hence A = 3.

solution:
Dependencies present in the program: write-after-write (WAW), read-after-write (RAW), and write-after-read (WAR).

The execution can be visualized with a pipeline diagram. The key is understanding the data hazards (dependencies) and how they are handled by stalls or forwarding.

  1. Instruction 1 (ADD): Enters the pipeline. No dependencies.

  2. Instruction 2 (MUL): Needs R2 from ADD.

  3. Instruction 3 (SUB): Needs R4 from MUL.

  • Cycles 1-3: Instructions are fetched and decoded.

  • Hazard 1 (ADD -> MUL): At the end of Cycle 3, the ADD instruction finishes its EX stage. Operand forwarding sends the R2 result directly to the MUL instruction's EX stage. This allows MUL to start its 3-cycle execution (EX1) in Cycle 4 with no stall.

title: Which of the following pipeline hazards can stall the pipeline
subject: COA
text: Which of the following pipeline hazards can stall the pipeline ?
solution: Pipeline hazards are conditions that prevent the next instruction from executing in its designated clock cycle. All three types of pipeline hazards (structural, control, and data) can cause stalls in a processor pipeline.

optionFeedback.html: Structural hazards occur when hardware resources are insufficient for concurrent instruction execution, causing pipeline stalls. Check if multiple instructions need the same functional unit simultaneously.
Control hazards arise from branch instructions that disrupt instruction flow, requiring pipeline stalls for resolution. Verify whether the option explains how branches affect sequential execution.

Data hazards occur when instructions depend on results from previous instructions not yet available. Check if other hazard types like structural or control also cause stalls before selecting this option.
Control hazards arise from branch instructions, while data hazards happen due to instruction dependencies. All three types can stall the pipeline execution flow.

title: Which of the following are NOT true in pipelined processor
subject: COA
text:
Which of the following statements are NOT true in a pipelined processor?

I. Bypassing can handle all RAW hazards.

II. Register renaming can eliminate all register-carried WAR hazards.

III. Control hazard penalties can be eliminated by dynamic branch prediction.
solution:
CONCEPT

Pipeline-hazard remedies address different constraints. Forwarding resolves a RAW dependency only when the producer value is available in time; register renaming removes name dependences such as WAR; branch prediction speculates on control flow but must recover from a wrong prediction.

APPLICATION

  1. Statement I: A load-use pair can need a stall because the loaded value becomes available after the immediately following consumer needs its execute-stage input. Therefore, bypassing does not handle every RAW hazard.

  2. Statement II: Assigning a new physical destination to a later write prevents it from overwriting the architectural name before an earlier read. Thus register renaming can eliminate register-carried WAR hazards.

  3. Statement III: Dynamic prediction reduces average control stalls, but a misprediction still flushes younger speculative instructions and redirects fetch. Therefore, it cannot eliminate every control-hazard penalty.

CROSS-CHECK / CONTRAST

  • I and II only combines one unsupported universal claim with one valid renaming claim.

  • II and III only combines the valid renaming claim with an unsupported prediction claim.

  • All of these would require the renaming claim to be false, although renaming removes the relevant name dependence.

Result: Statements I and III are NOT true, so the answer is I and III only.

optionFeedback.html: An immediate load consumer can need a bubble because the memory value arrives after its execute input is due, whereas a renamed destination removes the antidependence caused by architectural-name reuse.
An immediate load consumer can need a bubble because the memory value arrives after its execute input is due, while a branch misprediction flushes younger speculative work before fetch restarts.
A renamed destination removes the antidependence caused by architectural-name reuse, while a branch misprediction flushes younger speculative work before fetch restarts.
Forwarding depends on producer-result timing, renaming separates architectural-name reuse, and prediction still requires recovery whenever the predicted control path is wrong.

title: Register renaming is done in pipelined processors
subject: COA
text: Register renaming is done in pipelined processors

options.html: as an alternative to register allocation at compile time
for efficient access to function parameters and local variables

solution: Register renaming is a hardware technique used in pipelined processors to eliminate false dependencies (WAR and WAW hazards) by mapping architectural registers to a larger set of physical registers.

optionFeedback.html: This option confuses hardware register renaming with compiler-based allocation. Register renaming occurs at runtime to resolve hazards, not as a substitute for compile-time optimization strategies.
This option describes a different optimization goal. Register renaming targets pipeline hazards like WAR and WAW dependencies, not parameter or local variable access efficiency.
Register renaming eliminates false dependencies like WAR and WAW hazards by mapping architectural registers to physical ones.
Register renaming eliminates false data dependencies like WAR and WAW hazards, not address translation.

title: The expression for machine which is having m-bit instructions that
subject: COA
text: A machine uses m-bit instructions and supports zero-address, one-address, and two-address formats. Its memory contains 2p words. Assume every m-bit pattern encodes one of these instructions. If r, s, and t denote the numbers of zero-address, one-address, and two-address instructions, respectively, which expression relates m, p, r, s, and t?
solution:
Concept

A fixed m-bit instruction word has 2m possible bit patterns. A p-bit address field has 2p possible values.

Independent address fields multiply the number of complete instruction patterns, while an instruction format with no address field contributes one pattern per opcode.

Application

  1. Because the memory has 2p words, one memory address requires p bits.

  2. Each of the r zero-address instructions has no address field, so this class contributes r patterns.

  3. Each of the s one-address instructions can use any of 2p addresses, so this class contributes s · 2p patterns.

  4. Each of the t two-address instructions has two independent p-bit addresses, so this class contributes t · 2p · 2p = t · 22p patterns.

  5. These disjoint classes fill the m-bit instruction space, giving 2m = r + s · 2p + t · 22p.

Cross-check

When p = 0, each address field has one possible value and the expression reduces to 2m = r + s + t. This matches the one-word-memory case, where address fields add no extra choices.

Result: 2m = r + s · 2p + t · 22p.

optionFeedback.html: If p increases by 1 while r, s, and t stay fixed, this expression multiplies its entire right-hand side by 2. This shows that all three instruction counts share the same dependence on address width.

If p increases by 1 while r, s, and t stay fixed, this expression multiplies the r, s, and t terms by 2, 4, and 8, respectively. The three terms therefore scale with one, two, and three address-space factors.
If p increases by 1 while r, s, and t stay fixed, this expression multiplies the r, s, and t terms by 4, 2, and 1, respectively. The dependence on address width decreases across the three terms.

If p increases by 1 while r, s, and t stay fixed, this expression multiplies the r, s, and t terms by 1, 2, and 4, respectively. The dependence on address width grows once for each additional address field.

title: Processor has integer registers and floating point registers It uses
subject: COA
text: A processor has 16 integer registers (R0, R1, …, R15) and 64 floating point registers (F0, F1, …, F63). It uses a 2-byte instruction format. There are four categories of instructions: Type-1, Type-2, Type-3 and Type-4.Type-1 category consists of two instructions, each with 2 integer register operands and one floating point register operand(2Rs+1F). Type-2 category consists of eight instructions, each with 2 integer register operands (2Rs). Type-3 category consists of 14 instructions, each with one integer register operand and one floating point register operand (1R+1F). Type-4 category consists of N instructions, each with a floating point register operand (1F). The maximum value of N is ________.
solution:
Instruction size = 2−byte.

So, the total number of instruction encodings = 2^16

There are 16 possible integer registers, so no. of bits required for an integer operand = 4

There are 64 possible floating-point registers, so no. of bits required for a floating-point operand = 6

Type-1 instructions:

There are 2 type-1 instructions and each takes 2 integer operands and one floating point operand

No. of encodings consumed by type-1 = 2 × 2^4 × 2^4 × 2^6 =2^15.

Type-2 instructions:

There are 8 type-2 instructions and each takes 2 integer operands.

No. of encodings consumed by Type-2 instructions = 8 × 2^4 x 2^4 = 2^11.

Type-3 instructions:

There are 14 type-3 instructions and each takes one integer operand and one floating point operand.

No. of encodings consumed by Type-3 instructions = 14 × 2^4 x 2^6 = 14336.

So, no. of encodings left for Type-4 = 2^16 − (2^15 + 2^11 + 14336) = 16384.

Since type-4 instructions take one floating point register, no. of different instructions of Type-4 = 16384 / 64 = 256.

subject: COA

solution:
Answer: 4 instructions.

Explanation:

  1. Load A into the accumulator: ACC ← M[A]. This brings A from memory into the accumulator (1 instruction).

  3. Multiply the accumulator by C: ACC ← ACC * M[C]. This performs the multiplication using the accumulator (1 instruction).

  4. Store the result into X: M[X] ← ACC. Write the final result from the accumulator back to memory (1 instruction).

Total instructions = 4 (load, add, multiply, store).

Evaluate the sequence: PUSH 10; PUSH 30; ADD; PUSH 25; SUB; PUSH 22; MUL;

title: Consider system with 16-bit instructions and 6-bit addresses. If there
subject: COA
text: Consider a system with 16-bit instructions and 6-bit addresses. If there are 14 2-address instructions and 100 1-address instructions, what is the maximum number of 0-address instructions that can be formulated?
solution:
Concept

In an expanding-opcode design, an instruction format with fewer address fields frees bits that can extend the opcode.

If an address field has a bits, each unused opcode prefix at one level expands into 2a longer prefixes at the next level.

Application

  1. A 2-address instruction uses 2 × 6 = 12 address bits, leaving 16 − 12 = 4 opcode bits. Therefore, there are 24 = 16 possible 2-address opcode prefixes.

  2. Fourteen of these prefixes are assigned, so 16 − 14 = 2 prefixes remain available for expansion.

  3. For a 1-address instruction, each remaining prefix gains 6 opcode bits. This produces 2 × 26 = 128 possible 1-address opcode patterns.

  4. After assigning 100 of those patterns, 128 − 100 = 28 expanded prefixes remain for 0-address instructions.

  5. A 0-address instruction uses all 16 bits as opcode bits, so each of the 28 remaining prefixes gains the final 6 bits: 28 × 26 = 28 × 64 = 1792.

Cross-check

The complete 16-bit code space has 216 patterns. The assigned instructions consume 14 × 212 + 100 × 26 patterns, leaving 216 − 14 × 212 − 100 × 26 = 1792 patterns.

Therefore, the maximum number of 0-address instructions is 1792.

For 1653, the complete code-space count is 14 × 4096 + 100 × 64 + 1653 = 65397 instruction patterns.
For 1590, the complete code-space count is 14 × 4096 + 100 × 64 + 1590 = 65334 instruction patterns.
For 1903, the complete code-space count is 14 × 4096 + 100 × 64 + 1903 = 65647 instruction patterns.
